deep_dives.bottom_line: In this large randomized controlled trial, physiotherapist-led care for uncomplicated musculoskeletal conditions in the emergency department was found to be effective, safe, and cost-effective compared to usual physician- or nurse practitioner-led care, suggesting that physiotherapists can play a key role in improving emergency department efficiency and patient outcomes for these conditions.
deep_dives.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: Physiotherapist-led care in the emergency department for uncomplicated musculoskeletal conditions reduces length of stay, is safe, and is cost-effective compared to usual care.

- Study type: Open-label, pragmatic, randomized controlled trial with economic evaluation
- Population/setting: Adults aged 18 years and older with uncomplicated musculoskeletal conditions presenting to five emergency departments in New South Wales, Australia
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Physiotherapist-led care versus usual physician-led or nurse practitioner-led care
- Primary endpoints: Length of stay in the emergency department (time from arrival to discharge)
- Key results: Mean length of stay was 2.4 hours in the intervention group versus 3.4 hours in the control group (difference -1.0 h, 95% CI -1.2 to -0.8); adverse events were similar between groups (6.6% vs 5.9%, p=0.72); intervention group had lower costs (-$35.1, 95% CI -69.0 to -1.7) and a 98.1% probability of being cost-effective.
- Limitations:
- Open-label design may introduce performance bias
- Conducted only in New South Wales, Australia, which may limit generalizability
- Why this matters: Implementing physiotherapist-led care in emergency departments can improve efficiency and reduce costs without compromising patient safety for musculoskeletal presentations.
deep_dives.title: Physiotherapist-led care for musculoskeletal conditions in the emergency department (RESHAP-ED): a randomised controlled trial with economic evaluation.

deep_dives.bottom_line: In this large prospective cohort study, adding CT-based body composition metrics (skeletal muscle area, muscle radiodensity, and subcutaneous fat radiodensity) to standard risk models improved prediction of 30-day postoperative cardiovascular events in patients undergoing major noncardiac surgery, suggesting these imaging biomarkers may enhance preoperative risk stratification.
deep_dives.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: CT-derived body composition metrics enhance the prediction of postoperative cardiovascular events beyond conventional clinical predictors in patients undergoing major noncardiac surgery.

- Study type: Prospective cohort study
- Population/setting: Patients with cardiovascular disease or risk factors undergoing major noncardiac surgery in the multicenter PREVENGE-CB cohort and its Nanfang extension (N=1,594).
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Addition of CT-based body composition metrics (skeletal muscle area, muscle radiodensity, subcutaneous fat radiodensity) to standard clinical risk models versus standard clinical risk models alone.
- Primary endpoints: Composite cardiovascular events within 30 days after surgery.
- Key results: The addition of three CT-based body composition metrics improved discrimination for postoperative cardiovascular events over the Revised Cardiac Risk Index (ΔAUC = 0.136; 95% CI, 0.083 to 0.188), Gupta risk calculator (ΔAUC = 0.032; 95% CI, -0.002 to 0.065), and a refitted clinical model (ΔAUC = 0.035; 95% CI, 0.008 to 0.062); findings were validated in an independent cohort.
- Limitations:
- Potential generalizability limitations due to study population.
- CT imaging may not be routinely available for all surgical candidates.
- The study does not address cost-effectiveness or implementation feasibility.
- Why this matters: Incorporating CT-based body composition analysis into preoperative assessment may improve cardiovascular risk stratification and guide perioperative management.
deep_dives.title: Computed Tomography-based Body Composition Assessment for Preoperative Cardiovascular Risk Prediction: A Prospective Cohort Study.

deep_dives.bottom_line: In this large, post hoc analysis of two clinical trials, intraoperative corticosteroids at antiemetic doses did not significantly reduce postoperative pulmonary complications in major surgery patients, though a modest improvement in oxygenation was observed; these findings suggest routine corticosteroid use for pulmonary protection is not supported.
deep_dives.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: Intraoperative corticosteroid administration at antiemetic doses did not reduce postoperative pulmonary complications in adults undergoing major abdominal or thoracic surgery, though it modestly improved postoperative pulmonary gas exchange.

- Study type: Post hoc analysis of two clinical trials
- Population/setting: Adult patients undergoing major abdominal or thoracic surgeries across 30 hospitals (N=1963)
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Intraoperative corticosteroid administration at antiemetic doses versus no corticosteroid administration
- Primary endpoints: Composite of postoperative pulmonary complications within 30 days after surgery
- Key results: After weighting for confounders, corticosteroids were not associated with a significant reduction in postoperative pulmonary complications (OR 0.86, 95% CI 0.62-1.18, P=0.347); however, there was a modest improvement in arterial oxygenation (adjusted mean difference 19.9 mm Hg, 95% CI 0.64-39.1, P=0.043).
- Limitations:
- Post hoc analysis design
- Potential residual confounding despite weighting
- Findings may not generalize beyond major abdominal or thoracic surgeries
- Why this matters: This study informs perioperative management by showing that routine intraoperative corticosteroids at antiemetic doses do not reduce pulmonary complications, supporting their safety but not efficacy for this outcome.
deep_dives.title: Intraoperative corticosteroid administration and postoperative pulmonary complications: a secondary analysis of the iPROVE clinical trials.

deep_dives.bottom_line: In this multicenter randomized controlled trial, a structured early mobilization program for mechanically ventilated patients with sepsis or acute respiratory failure did not improve functional status at ICU discharge or long-term recovery compared to usual care, suggesting that while early mobilization is feasible and increases activity, it may not confer additional functional benefit in this population.
deep_dives.deep_dive_markdown:
**BOTTOM LINE:** In this multicenter randomized controlled trial, a structured early mobilization program for mechanically ventilated patients with sepsis or acute respiratory failure did not improve functional status at ICU discharge or long-term recovery compared to usual care, suggesting that while early mobilization is feasible and increases activity, it may not confer additional functional benefit in this population.

BOTTOM LINE: A structured early mobilization program for mechanically ventilated patients with sepsis or acute respiratory failure did not improve functional status at ICU discharge or at 12 months compared to usual care.

- Study type: Multicenter randomized open-label controlled trial
- Population/setting: Adult patients with sepsis or respiratory failure requiring invasive ventilation for ≥48 hours in five tertiary hospitals in South Korea
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Structured six-step early mobilization program versus usual care
- Primary endpoints: Functional Status Score for the ICU (FSS-ICU) at ICU discharge
- Key results: No significant difference in FSS-ICU at ICU discharge between groups (mean 23.6 vs. 22.2; P = 0.44); intervention group mobilized earlier and more often; long-term outcomes improved similarly in both groups over 12 months.
- Limitations:
- Open-label design may introduce bias
- Study conducted only in South Korea, limiting generalizability
- Sample size may limit detection of small differences
- Why this matters: This study challenges the assumption that protocolized early mobilization improves short- or long-term functional outcomes in mechanically ventilated ICU patients, informing ICU rehabilitation practices.
deep_dives.title: Early mobilization for mechanical ventilation for sepsis or acute respiratory failure (EVER): a multicenter randomized controlled trial with 12-month outcomes.

deep_dives.bottom_line: This randomized controlled trial found that moderate to deep neuromuscular blockade significantly reduces both the incidence and severity of the oculocardiac reflex during pediatric strabismus surgery compared to minimal to shallow blockade, suggesting that deeper blockade may improve intraoperative cardiac safety in this population.
deep_dives.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: Moderate to deep neuromuscular blockade significantly reduces the incidence and severity of the oculocardiac reflex during pediatric strabismus surgery compared to minimal to shallow blockade.

- Study type: Prospective, double-blinded randomized controlled trial
- Population/setting: 204 pediatric patients aged 3 to 18 years undergoing strabismus surgery under general anesthesia
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Moderate to deep neuromuscular blockade (train-of-four count 0 to 3) versus minimal to shallow neuromuscular blockade (train-of-four count of 4 with ratio less than 0.9)
- Primary endpoints: Incidence of oculocardiac reflex grade greater than or equal to 2 (heart rate decrease ≥20% from baseline)
- Key results: OCR grade ≥2 occurred less in the moderate to deep group (30.3%) than the minimal to shallow group (53.9%; OR 0.37, 95% CI 0.21–0.66, P=0.001); severe OCR (grade ≥3) was also reduced (18.2% vs 35.3%; OR 0.41, 95% CI 0.21–0.78, P=0.007); magnitude and duration of heart rate reduction were both smaller in the moderate to deep group.
- Limitations:
- Single surgical procedure and pediatric population may limit generalizability.
- No long-term outcomes reported.
- Why this matters: Optimizing neuromuscular blockade depth can reduce the risk and severity of oculocardiac reflex, improving safety during pediatric strabismus surgery.
deep_dives.title: Neuromuscular Blockade Depth and Oculocardiac Reflex in Pediatric Strabismus Surgery: A Randomized Clinical Trial.

pubmed.title: Predictive Power of Pulmonary Artery Stiffness - Right Ventricular Interplay, but not Pulmonary Vascular Resistance, in Mild Pulmonary Hypertension: A PVRI GoDeep meta-registry analysis.

pubmed.title: Cognition, Quality of Life, and Psychological Outcomes in Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest Survivors - Results from the German Cardiac Arrest Registry (G-CAR).

pubmed.title: Prehospital Emergency Cricothyroidotomy in Denmark: A Nationwide Cohort Study, 2016-2023.

pubmed.journal: American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine
pubmed.title: Impact of a Large-Scale Mold Intervention in Public Housing on Asthma Emergency Department Visits.

pubmed.bottom_line: This state-of-the-art review highlights that while β-blockers have established benefits in certain acute critical care scenarios, their use in broader critical illness remains controversial due to limited and conflicting evidence, with significant gaps in knowledge regarding patient selection, optimal timing, and safety; thus, a personalized, physiology-guided approach is recommended until stronger randomized data are available.
pubmed.title: State-of-the-art review: ß-blockade in critical illness.

deep_dives.bottom_line: This moderate-certainty meta-analysis of 10 randomized trials found that intravenous lidocaine modestly reduces pain and opioid use after adult spine surgery, with clinically meaningful benefits primarily in patients undergoing instrumented fusion or complex procedures; its routine use may be most justified in these higher-risk surgeries.
deep_dives.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: Perioperative intravenous lidocaine reduces postoperative pain and opioid consumption in adult spine surgery, with the greatest benefit seen in instrumented fusion and complex procedures.

- Study type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
- Population/setting: Adults undergoing spine surgery, based on 10 randomized trials
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Perioperative intravenous lidocaine infusion versus placebo or standard care
- Primary endpoints: Postoperative pain intensity at 24 hours

deep_dives.bottom_line: This new American College of Chest Physicians guideline provides evidence-based recommendations—mostly of moderate to low certainty—for initiating tobacco treatment in hospitalized patients, emphasizing an opt-out approach with proactive counseling and pharmacotherapy; while high-certainty evidence is lacking, these recommendations aim to standardize and improve inpatient tobacco cessation efforts, addressing a major opportunity for intervention.
deep_dives.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: This guideline provides evidence-based recommendations for tobacco treatment in hospitalized patients, emphasizing proactive counseling and pharmacotherapy to improve cessation outcomes.

- Study type: Clinical practice guideline based on systematic review and evidence appraisal (GRADE methodology).
- Population/setting: Hospitalized patients who smoke in the United States; recommendations developed by a multidisciplinary panel.
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Opt-out, population-based tobacco treatment (counseling and pharmacotherapy) versus usual care or no intervention.
- Primary endpoints: Smoking cessation outcomes, hospital readmissions, and costs.
- Key results: Eight recommendations were made: four supported by moderate-certainty evidence, two by low-certainty, and two by very low-certainty evidence; no recommendations were supported by high-certainty evidence specific to inpatient settings.
- Limitations:
- No high-certainty evidence specific to inpatient tobacco treatment.
- Some recommendations rely on low or very low-certainty evidence and expert consensus.
- Optimal implementation strategies and cost-effectiveness remain unclear.
- Why this matters: Guidance is needed to standardize and improve tobacco treatment for hospitalized patients, potentially reducing morbidity, readmissions, and healthcare costs.
deep_dives.title: Tobacco Treatment in the Inpatient Setting: An American College of Chest Physicians Clinical Practice Guideline.

deep_dives.bottom_line: This large registry study found that while pulseless electrical activity (PEA) and asystole differ in short-term outcomes during pediatric in-hospital cardiac arrest, the survival difference is mainly seen in neonates and NICU events, with no significant survival difference between rhythms in older children—suggesting that grouping these rhythms as “non-shockable” may be appropriate outside the neonatal population.
deep_dives.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: PEA and asystole as initial rhythms in pediatric IHCA have different short-term outcomes, but survival differences are mainly seen in neonates and NICU events, not in older children.

- Study type: Retrospective cohort study using registry data
- Population/setting: Pediatric (<18 years) in-hospital cardiac arrest cases from the American Heart Association GWTG-Resuscitation registry (2000-2023)
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Initial pulseless rhythm of PEA versus asystole
- Primary endpoints: Return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), restoration of circulation (ROC, defined as ROSC or ROC with ECMO), and survival to hospital discharge
- Key results: Asystole was associated with lower odds of ROSC (aOR 0.70, 95% CI 0.64-0.77), ROC (aOR 0.71, 95% CI 0.64-0.78), and survival to discharge (aOR 0.89, 95% CI 0.81-0.99) compared to PEA; survival differences were not significant in older children or after excluding NICU events.
- Limitations:
- Retrospective design
- Potential for unmeasured confounding
- Registry data may have variable data quality
- Results may not generalize outside registry hospitals
- Why this matters: Understanding differences between PEA and asystole in pediatric IHCA can inform resuscitation strategies and prognostication, especially in neonates and NICU settings.
deep_dives.title: Pulseless electrical activity versus asystole as initial pulseless rhythm in children: challenging convention regarding non-shockable rhythms.

deep_dives.bottom_line: In this randomized study of adults with severe OSA, expiratory pressure alleviation (EPA) during CPAP therapy impaired upper airway patency, required higher CPAP pressures, and resulted in higher residual AHI without improving adherence, suggesting that EPA may compromise CPAP effectiveness in this population.
deep_dives.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: Expiratory pressure alleviation (EPA) during CPAP therapy impairs upper airway patency and OSA control, requiring higher CPAP pressures, but does not affect adherence.

- Study type: Randomized crossover study
- Population/setting: Adults with severe OSA (N=29; 55% female; age 63±12 years; BMI 37±7 kg/m2; AHI 58 (39-83) events/h) using nasal CPAP, studied in-lab and at home.
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: CPAP with EPA activation versus CPAP without EPA activation.
- Primary endpoints: Peak inspiratory flow (PIF), titrated CPAP level, residual apnea-hypopnea index (AHI), and CPAP adherence.
- Key results: EPA reduced PIF (0.19 vs 0.38 L/s, P<0.001), required higher CPAP pressures (11.40 vs 9.17 cmH2O, P<0.001), and increased residual AHI during both fixed (3.7 vs 1.3 events/h) and auto-CPAP (1.4 vs 0.8 events/h, P<0.05), with no significant difference in adherence.
- Limitations:
- Small sample size (N=29).
- Short-term assessment; long-term outcomes not evaluated.
- Single-center study.
- Why this matters: Understanding the impact of EPA on airway patency and OSA control is crucial for optimizing CPAP therapy and device selection in patients with severe OSA.
deep_dives.title: Impairment of upper airway patency and CPAP effectiveness during obstructive sleep apnea treatment with expiratory pressure alleviation: a randomized study.

deep_dives.bottom_line: In this phase 2 randomized trial of fit adults with newly diagnosed AML (excluding certain favorable genotypes), azacitidine plus venetoclax significantly improved event-free survival and had fewer severe infections and hemorrhages compared to standard induction chemotherapy, suggesting this less intensive regimen may be a preferable frontline option for many patients.
deep_dives.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: Azacitidine plus venetoclax significantly improved event-free survival compared to induction chemotherapy in induction-eligible adults with AML, with fewer severe infections and hemorrhages.

- Study type: Multicenter, phase 2, randomized controlled trial
- Population/setting: Previously untreated adults with AML eligible for induction chemotherapy, excluding those with core binding factor fusions, FLT3 mutations, or NPM1 mutations (unless age ≥60), across multiple centers; N=172, median age 64, 72% with adverse-risk disease.
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Azacitidine plus venetoclax versus standard induction chemotherapy
- Primary endpoints: Event-free survival
- Key results: Median event-free survival was 14.5 months in the azacitidine-venetoclax group versus 6.2 months in the induction chemotherapy group (hazard ratio for event or death, 0.57; P=0.002); grade 3 or higher infections occurred in 28% vs 41%, and grade 3 or higher hemorrhage in 2% vs 12%, respectively.
- Limitations:
- Phase 2 trial with moderate sample size
- Exclusion of patients with certain genetic mutations limits generalizability
- Median follow-up of 21.9 months may not capture long-term outcomes
- Why this matters: These findings suggest azacitidine plus venetoclax may be a more effective and safer alternative to induction chemotherapy for eligible AML patients, potentially changing standard treatment approaches.
deep_dives.journal: The New England journal of medicine
deep_dives.title: Azacitidine-Venetoclax or Induction Chemotherapy for Acute Myeloid Leukemia.

cybermed_stored_deep_dive.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: Expiratory pressure alleviation (EPA) during CPAP therapy impairs upper airway patency and OSA control, requiring higher CPAP pressures, but does not affect adherence.

- Study type: Randomized crossover study
- Population/setting: Adults with severe OSA (N=29; 55% female; age 63±12 years; BMI 37±7 kg/m2; AHI 58 (39-83) events/h) using nasal CPAP, studied in-lab and at home.
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: CPAP with EPA activation versus CPAP without EPA activation.
- Primary endpoints: Peak inspiratory flow (PIF), titrated CPAP level, residual apnea-hypopnea index (AHI), and CPAP adherence.
- Key results: EPA reduced PIF (0.19 vs 0.38 L/s, P<0.001), required higher CPAP pressures (11.40 vs 9.17 cmH2O, P<0.001), and increased residual AHI during both fixed (3.7 vs 1.3 events/h) and auto-CPAP (1.4 vs 0.8 events/h, P<0.05), with no significant difference in adherence.
- Limitations:
- Small sample size (N=29).
- Short-term assessment; long-term outcomes not evaluated.
- Single-center study.
- Why this matters: Understanding the impact of EPA on airway patency and OSA control is crucial for optimizing CPAP therapy and device selection in patients with severe OSA.

cybermed_stored_deep_dive.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: Azacitidine plus venetoclax significantly improved event-free survival compared to induction chemotherapy in induction-eligible adults with AML, with fewer severe infections and hemorrhages.

- Study type: Multicenter, phase 2, randomized controlled trial
- Population/setting: Previously untreated adults with AML eligible for induction chemotherapy, excluding those with core binding factor fusions, FLT3 mutations, or NPM1 mutations (unless age ≥60), across multiple centers; N=172, median age 64, 72% with adverse-risk disease.
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Azacitidine plus venetoclax versus standard induction chemotherapy
- Primary endpoints: Event-free survival
- Key results: Median event-free survival was 14.5 months in the azacitidine-venetoclax group versus 6.2 months in the induction chemotherapy group (hazard ratio for event or death, 0.57; P=0.002); grade 3 or higher infections occurred in 28% vs 41%, and grade 3 or higher hemorrhage in 2% vs 12%, respectively.
- Limitations:
- Phase 2 trial with moderate sample size
- Exclusion of patients with certain genetic mutations limits generalizability
- Median follow-up of 21.9 months may not capture long-term outcomes
- Why this matters: These findings suggest azacitidine plus venetoclax may be a more effective and safer alternative to induction chemotherapy for eligible AML patients, potentially changing standard treatment approaches.

deep_dives.bottom_line: This moderate-certainty meta-analysis of 38 RCTs found that perioperative selective COX-2 inhibitors modestly reduce acute pain-related interference with daily living after surgery and may lower chronic pain incidence, supporting their use for improved postoperative recovery beyond simple pain intensity measures.
deep_dives.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: Perioperative selective COX-2 inhibitors likely provide a clinically meaningful reduction in acute pain-related interference with daily function after surgery and may improve chronic pain incidence and quality of recovery, without clear evidence of increased adverse events.

- Study type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
- Population/setting: Adults undergoing any type of surgical procedure in single- and multicenter randomized controlled trials (N=5,424; mean age 48 years; 65% female; various surgical specialties and anesthesia types)
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Systemic perioperative selective COX-2 inhibitors (oral or intravenous) versus placebo, opioids, or usual care
- Primary endpoints: Postoperative acute pain assessed using validated multidimensional instruments evaluating pain-related interference with daily living within 1 month after surgery
- Key results: Selective COX-2 inhibitors reduced acute pain-related interference (Brief Pain Inventory mean difference -1.1, 95% CI -1.4 to -0.8; moderate certainty), increased the proportion achieving a clinically important analgesic effect by 19% (95% CI 7% to 32%), reduced chronic pain incidence (OR 0.44, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.93; low certainty), improved quality of recovery (QoR-9 mean difference 0.84, 95% CI 0.33 to 1.35; low certainty), and lowered intraoperative blood loss (mean difference -22 ml, 95% CI -40 to -4; low certainty), with no significant differences in other adverse events.
- Limitations:
- Certainty of evidence was moderate to very low for most outcomes due to risk of bias, imprecision, and inconsistency.
- Most included RCTs had some concerns or high risk of bias.
- Heterogeneity in surgical procedures, COX-2 inhibitor types, dosing, and timing.
- Limited data on long-term outcomes and adverse events.
- Publication bias could not be assessed.
- Why this matters: This study supports the use of selective COX-2 inhibitors for perioperative pain management to improve patient-centered recovery outcomes, with no clear increase in major adverse events, informing clinicians about their effectiveness and safety profile in surgical patients.
deep_dives.title: Effectiveness of Selective Cyclooxygenase-2 Inhibitors for Postoperative Pain Management Using Multidimensional Pain Assessment: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.

deep_dives.bottom_line: In this large cluster randomized crossover trial, initiating resuscitation with 30% oxygen versus room air in moderate- to late-preterm infants (32–35 weeks) did not significantly affect the need for ongoing respiratory support or most secondary outcomes, suggesting that starting with room air is as effective as higher oxygen for this group. This supports current practice and may help avoid unnecessary oxygen exposure in preterm infants.

BOTTOM LINE: Initiating resuscitation with Fio2 0.30 versus 0.21 in moderate- to late-preterm infants did not affect the proportion still receiving respiratory support when leaving the delivery room.

- Study type: Unblinded, cluster randomized crossover trial
- Population/setting: Neonates born at 32 to 35 weeks' gestation in 26 Australian maternity hospitals who commenced respiratory support within 3 minutes of birth.
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Initial Fio2 of 0.30 versus initial Fio2 of 0.21 during the first 3 minutes of delivery room respiratory support.
- Primary endpoints: Ongoing respiratory support when leaving the delivery room.
- Key results: Ongoing respiratory support when leaving the delivery room occurred in 72.6% (Fio2 0.30) vs 73.3% (Fio2 0.21) (risk difference, -0.83 [95% CI, -4.33 to 2.67]); most secondary outcomes were not significantly different, but Fio2 0.30 reduced need for higher levels of support and endotracheal ventilation beyond the delivery room.
- Limitations:
- Unblinded design may introduce bias.
- Cluster randomization at the site level may affect generalizability.
- Waiver of informed consent could impact ethical considerations.
- Why this matters: This study informs optimal oxygen administration strategies for moderate- to late-preterm infants requiring resuscitation, suggesting no difference in primary outcome but potential benefits in reducing escalation of respiratory support.
deep_dives.title: Oxygen vs Air at Birth for Moderate- to Late-Preterm Infants: The AIROPLANE Cluster Randomized Crossover Trial.

deep_dives.bottom_line: This meta-analysis of 20 randomized trials (2342 patients) found that reductions in intraoperative hypotension with HPI-guided management are typically associated with increased hemodynamic treatment intensity, suggesting that the benefit of HPI may be due to more aggressive intervention rather than superior prediction; clinicians should weigh the risks and benefits of increased treatment when using HPI protocols.
deep_dives.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: Reduction of hypotension in HPI-guided management trials is generally associated with increased hemodynamic treatment intensity.

- Study type: Meta-analysis of randomized trials
- Population/setting: Twenty randomized trials including 2342 patients undergoing HPI-guided hypotension prevention interventions
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: HPI-guided hypotension prevention versus MAP alert-based management (MAP 65 mmHg threshold)
- Primary endpoints: Statistically significant reduction in hypotension and statistically significant increases in hemodynamic treatment (fluids, vasopressors, or inotropes)
- Key results: Among 13 trials with hypotension reduction, 69% reported greater treatment intensity in the HPI group; no increased treatment intensity was seen in trials without hypotension reduction; reduction of hypotension was significantly associated with greater treatment intensity (p = 0.029); TWA differences correlated with treatment intensity (p < 0.001).
- Limitations:
- Meta-analysis relies on published data, which may be heterogeneous.
- Treatment intensity definitions and reporting may vary across trials.
- Potential for publication bias.
- Why this matters: Understanding that reduced hypotension with HPI-guided management is often achieved through more intensive hemodynamic interventions informs clinicians about the trade-offs between hypotension prevention and treatment burden.
deep_dives.title: Associations between reduction of hypotension and treatment intensity in hypotension prediction index studies.

deep_dives.bottom_line: Two phase 3 randomized, placebo-controlled trials show that oveporexton, an oral orexin receptor 2 agonist, significantly improves wakefulness, reduces sleepiness, and markedly lowers cataplexy rates in patients with narcolepsy type 1 over 12 weeks, providing strong evidence for its efficacy and potential as a new targeted therapy.
deep_dives.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: Oveporexton significantly improved wakefulness, reduced sleepiness, and decreased cataplexy in patients with narcolepsy type 1 over 12 weeks, but was associated with increased urinary frequency and transient insomnia.

- Study type: Two phase 3, randomized, placebo-controlled trials
- Population/setting: Participants aged 16 to 70 years with narcolepsy type 1, enrolled in multicenter trials (First Light: N=168; Radiant Light: N=105)
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Twice-daily oveporexton (1 mg or 2 mg) versus placebo
- Primary endpoints: Change from baseline to week 12 in mean sleep latency on the Maintenance of Wakefulness Test (MWT)
- Key results: Oveporexton increased mean sleep latency by 14.3 to 19.8 minutes versus -0.4 to -0.8 minutes with placebo (P<0.001); ESS scores improved by -9.7 to -11.8 versus -1.5 to -1.7 with placebo (P<0.001); weekly cataplexy rates reduced by 79.0% to 88.8% versus 27.7% to 39.1% with placebo (P<0.001); adverse events occurred in 86-89% with oveporexton versus 43-54% with placebo.
- Limitations:
- Short duration of 12 weeks
- High incidence of adverse events with oveporexton
- Long-term safety and efficacy not assessed
- Why this matters: Oveporexton offers a promising new oral treatment for narcolepsy type 1, addressing both excessive sleepiness and cataplexy, but clinicians should monitor for common side effects.

deep_dives.title: Oveporexton for Narcolepsy Type 1 - Results from Two Phase 3 Trials.

deep_dives.bottom_line: In this randomized controlled trial of 131 patients with fibrotic interstitial lung disease, high intensity interval training (HIIT) was as safe and effective as moderate intensity continuous training (MICT) for improving exercise endurance, suggesting HIIT is a viable alternative to standard PR exercise regimens in this population.
deep_dives.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: High intensity interval training (HIIT) is as effective and safe as moderate intensity continuous training (MICT) for improving exercise endurance in people with fibrotic interstitial lung disease (fILD), and may be considered as an alternative training modality.

- Study type: Randomized controlled trial
- Population/setting: 131 participants with fibrotic interstitial lung disease (fILD), stratified by exertional desaturation, in a pulmonary rehabilitation program
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: HIIT (high intensity interval training) versus MICT (moderate intensity continuous training) during an 8-week, twice-weekly pulmonary rehabilitation program
- Primary endpoints: Cycle endurance time
- Key results: Both HIIT and MICT led to clinically important improvements in cycle endurance time with no significant between-group difference (MD -63s, 95% CI -195 to 68s); similar results were observed for 6-minute walk distance (MD 4m, 95% CI -20 to 28m) and all secondary outcomes; no adverse events occurred in either group.
- Limitations:
- Single study population may limit generalizability
- Long-term outcomes beyond 6 months not reported
- Details on adherence outside supervised sessions not provided
- Why this matters: This study supports HIIT as a safe and effective alternative to standard MICT in pulmonary rehabilitation for fILD, offering flexibility in exercise prescription.

deep_dives.title: High intensity interval training in interstitial lung disease: a randomized controlled trial.

cybermed_stored_deep_dive.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: Perioperative selective COX-2 inhibitors likely provide a clinically meaningful reduction in acute pain-related interference with daily function after surgery and may improve chronic pain incidence and quality of recovery, without clear evidence of increased adverse events.

- Study type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
- Population/setting: Adults undergoing any type of surgical procedure in single- and multicenter randomized controlled trials (N=5,424; mean age 48 years; 65% female; various surgical specialties and anesthesia types)
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Systemic perioperative selective COX-2 inhibitors (oral or intravenous) versus placebo, opioids, or usual care
- Primary endpoints: Postoperative acute pain assessed using validated multidimensional instruments evaluating pain-related interference with daily living within 1 month after surgery
- Key results: Selective COX-2 inhibitors reduced acute pain-related interference (Brief Pain Inventory mean difference -1.1, 95% CI -1.4 to -0.8; moderate certainty), increased the proportion achieving a clinically important analgesic effect by 19% (95% CI 7% to 32%), reduced chronic pain incidence (OR 0.44, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.93; low certainty), improved quality of recovery (QoR-9 mean difference 0.84, 95% CI 0.33 to 1.35; low certainty), and lowered intraoperative blood loss (mean difference -22 ml, 95% CI -40 to -4; low certainty), with no significant differences in other adverse events.
- Limitations:
- Certainty of evidence was moderate to very low for most outcomes due to risk of bias, imprecision, and inconsistency.
- Most included RCTs had some concerns or high risk of bias.
- Heterogeneity in surgical procedures, COX-2 inhibitor types, dosing, and timing.
- Limited data on long-term outcomes and adverse events.
- Publication bias could not be assessed.
- Why this matters: This study supports the use of selective COX-2 inhibitors for perioperative pain management to improve patient-centered recovery outcomes, with no clear increase in major adverse events, informing clinicians about their effectiveness and safety profile in surgical patients.
cybermed_stored_deep_dive.title: Effectiveness of Selective Cyclooxygenase-2 Inhibitors for Postoperative Pain Management Using Multidimensional Pain Assessment: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.

BOTTOM LINE: Initiating resuscitation with Fio2 0.30 versus 0.21 in moderate- to late-preterm infants did not affect the proportion still receiving respiratory support when leaving the delivery room.

- Study type: Unblinded, cluster randomized crossover trial
- Population/setting: Neonates born at 32 to 35 weeks' gestation in 26 Australian maternity hospitals who commenced respiratory support within 3 minutes of birth.
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Initial Fio2 of 0.30 versus initial Fio2 of 0.21 during the first 3 minutes of delivery room respiratory support.
- Primary endpoints: Ongoing respiratory support when leaving the delivery room.
- Key results: Ongoing respiratory support when leaving the delivery room occurred in 72.6% (Fio2 0.30) vs 73.3% (Fio2 0.21) (risk difference, -0.83 [95% CI, -4.33 to 2.67]); most secondary outcomes were not significantly different, but Fio2 0.30 reduced need for higher levels of support and endotracheal ventilation beyond the delivery room.
- Limitations:
- Unblinded design may introduce bias.
- Cluster randomization at the site level may affect generalizability.
- Waiver of informed consent could impact ethical considerations.
- Why this matters: This study informs optimal oxygen administration strategies for moderate- to late-preterm infants requiring resuscitation, suggesting no difference in primary outcome but potential benefits in reducing escalation of respiratory support.
cybermed_stored_deep_dive.title: Oxygen vs Air at Birth for Moderate- to Late-Preterm Infants: The AIROPLANE Cluster Randomized Crossover Trial.

cybermed_stored_deep_dive.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: Reduction of hypotension in HPI-guided management trials is generally associated with increased hemodynamic treatment intensity.

- Study type: Meta-analysis of randomized trials
- Population/setting: Twenty randomized trials including 2342 patients undergoing HPI-guided hypotension prevention interventions
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: HPI-guided hypotension prevention versus MAP alert-based management (MAP 65 mmHg threshold)
- Primary endpoints: Statistically significant reduction in hypotension and statistically significant increases in hemodynamic treatment (fluids, vasopressors, or inotropes)
- Key results: Among 13 trials with hypotension reduction, 69% reported greater treatment intensity in the HPI group; no increased treatment intensity was seen in trials without hypotension reduction; reduction of hypotension was significantly associated with greater treatment intensity (p = 0.029); TWA differences correlated with treatment intensity (p < 0.001).
- Limitations:
- Meta-analysis relies on published data, which may be heterogeneous.
- Treatment intensity definitions and reporting may vary across trials.
- Potential for publication bias.
- Why this matters: Understanding that reduced hypotension with HPI-guided management is often achieved through more intensive hemodynamic interventions informs clinicians about the trade-offs between hypotension prevention and treatment burden.
cybermed_stored_deep_dive.title: Associations between reduction of hypotension and treatment intensity in hypotension prediction index studies.

cybermed_stored_deep_dive.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: Oveporexton significantly improved wakefulness, reduced sleepiness, and decreased cataplexy in patients with narcolepsy type 1 over 12 weeks, but was associated with increased urinary frequency and transient insomnia.

- Study type: Two phase 3, randomized, placebo-controlled trials
- Population/setting: Participants aged 16 to 70 years with narcolepsy type 1, enrolled in multicenter trials (First Light: N=168; Radiant Light: N=105)
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Twice-daily oveporexton (1 mg or 2 mg) versus placebo
- Primary endpoints: Change from baseline to week 12 in mean sleep latency on the Maintenance of Wakefulness Test (MWT)
- Key results: Oveporexton increased mean sleep latency by 14.3 to 19.8 minutes versus -0.4 to -0.8 minutes with placebo (P<0.001); ESS scores improved by -9.7 to -11.8 versus -1.5 to -1.7 with placebo (P<0.001); weekly cataplexy rates reduced by 79.0% to 88.8% versus 27.7% to 39.1% with placebo (P<0.001); adverse events occurred in 86-89% with oveporexton versus 43-54% with placebo.
- Limitations:
- Short duration of 12 weeks

- Study type: Randomized controlled trial
- Population/setting: 131 participants with fibrotic interstitial lung disease (fILD), stratified by exertional desaturation, in a pulmonary rehabilitation program
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: HIIT (high intensity interval training) versus MICT (moderate intensity continuous training) during an 8-week, twice-weekly pulmonary rehabilitation program
- Primary endpoints: Cycle endurance time
- Key results: Both HIIT and MICT led to clinically important improvements in cycle endurance time with no significant between-group difference (MD -63s, 95% CI -195 to 68s); similar results were observed for 6-minute walk distance (MD 4m, 95% CI -20 to 28m) and all secondary outcomes; no adverse events occurred in either group.

- Single study population may limit generalizability
- Long-term outcomes beyond 6 months not reported
- Details on adherence outside supervised sessions not provided
- Why this matters: This study supports HIIT as a safe and effective alternative to standard MICT in pulmonary rehabilitation for fILD, offering flexibility in exercise prescription.

deep_dives.bottom_line: This prospective, randomized study found that electromyographic monitoring of the abductor digiti minimi (ADM) and adductor pollicis (AP) muscles yields equivalent results for rocuronium onset and sugammadex recovery times overall, but right-hand ADM monitoring may show faster recovery than AP; this suggests either muscle can be reliably used for neuromuscular monitoring, though hand selection may influence recovery readings.
deep_dives.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: Electromyographic monitoring of the abductor digiti minimi (ADM) and adductor pollicis (AP) muscles provides equivalent results for neuromuscular block onset and recovery, except that ADM recovers faster than AP when monitored on the dominant (right) hand.

- Study type: Prospective, randomized trial
- Population/setting: 44 consenting patients undergoing general anesthesia with simultaneous EMG monitoring of ADM and AP muscles
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: EMG monitoring of ADM muscle versus AP muscle during rocuronium-induced neuromuscular block and sugammadex-induced recovery
- Primary endpoints: Onset time of neuromuscular block (rocuronium to TOF count=0), recovery time (sugammadex to TOF ratio ≥0.9), and time to maximal recovery (sugammadex to TOF ratio=1.0)
- Key results: No significant differences in onset or recovery times between ADM and AP overall; when monitored on the right hand, ADM recovered 93 s (25%) faster to TOF ≥0.9 and 105 s (20%) faster to TOF=1.0 than AP; no difference when monitored on the left hand.
- Limitations:
- Small sample size (44 patients)
- Single-center study
- Handedness and arm dominance may affect generalizability
- Why this matters: Findings support the use of either ADM or AP muscle for neuromuscular monitoring, with consideration of arm dominance for accurate recovery assessment.
deep_dives.title: Prospective, randomized comparison of electromyographic neuromuscular responses from the adductor pollicis and abductor digiti minimi muscles during rocuronium-induced neuromuscular block.

deep_dives.bottom_line: In this large randomized trial, increasing maternal intake of eggs and peanuts during pregnancy and lactation did not reduce the risk of egg or peanut allergy in high-risk infants at 1 year, indicating that this dietary strategy is not effective for allergy prevention in this population.
deep_dives.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: A maternal diet high in eggs and peanuts during pregnancy and lactation did not significantly reduce the risk of egg or peanut allergy in infants at 1 year of age compared to a standard diet.

- Study type: Multisite randomized trial
- Population/setting: Pregnant women with unborn children at high risk for allergic disease (at least two biologic family members with medically diagnosed allergic disease) across multiple sites.
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: High egg-peanut diet (≥6 eggs and 60 peanuts per week) versus standard diet (≤3 eggs and 30 peanuts per week) from before 23 weeks' gestation to 4 months postnatally.
- Primary endpoints: IgE-mediated egg or peanut allergy in the infant at 1 year of age.
- Key results: No significant difference in infant allergy rates: 7.8% in the high egg-peanut group vs. 8.4% in the standard-diet group (relative risk 0.93; 95% CI, 0.69 to 1.26; P = 0.65); safety measures were similar between groups.
- Limitations:
- Study limited to infants at high familial risk for allergy.
- Follow-up only until 1 year of age.
- Dietary adherence and allergen exposure outside the study protocol not fully controlled.
- Why this matters: This study provides evidence that increasing maternal intake of eggs and peanuts during pregnancy and lactation does not prevent egg or peanut allergy in high-risk infants, informing dietary recommendations for expectant and breastfeeding mothers.
deep_dives.journal: The New England journal of medicine
deep_dives.title: Trial of a Maternal Diet Rich in Eggs and Peanuts to Reduce Infant Allergy.

deep_dives.deep_dive_markdown:
**BOTTOM LINE:** In this multicenter, double-blind, randomized controlled trial of 370 nulliparous individuals, intrauterine instillation of mepivacaine did not significantly reduce pain during IUD placement compared to placebo, suggesting that this intervention does not provide clinically meaningful pain relief for IUD insertion in this population. This finding is important for guiding pain management strategies during IUD placement.

BOTTOM LINE: Intrauterine instillation of mepivacaine significantly reduced pain and improved tolerability during IUD placement in nulliparous individuals compared to placebo.

- Study type: Multicenter, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial
- Population/setting: Nulliparous individuals aged 18 to 31 years undergoing IUD placement at 11 outpatient clinics in Sweden
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Intrauterine instillation of 10 mL mepivacaine (20 mg/mL) versus 10 mL sodium chloride (placebo) 2 minutes before IUD placement
- Primary endpoints: Clinician-adjusted difference in pain scores during IUD placement measured on a 100-mm visual analog scale
- Key results: Mean pain score was 43.8 mm in the mepivacaine group vs 58.6 mm in the placebo group (mean difference, 14.8 mm; 95% CI, 10.0-19.6; P < .001); tolerable pain was reported by 98.3% in the mepivacaine group vs 91.4% in the placebo group (relative risk, 1.08; NNT, 15).
- Limitations:
- Study limited to nulliparous individuals aged 18-31 years.
- Only IUDs with smaller-diameter placement tubes were included.
- Exclusion of participants with certain conditions may limit generalizability.
- Why this matters: Reducing pain during IUD placement may increase patient satisfaction and support informed contraceptive choices, potentially improving uptake of IUDs among young, nulliparous individuals.
deep_dives.title: Intrauterine Mepivacaine Instillation vs Placebo for Pain During IUD Placement: A Randomized Clinical Trial.

deep_dives.bottom_line: In this large interim analysis, extending colonoscopy surveillance intervals from 3 to 5 years after high-risk adenoma removal was noninferior to the current 3-year interval in terms of 5-year colorectal cancer incidence, suggesting that less frequent surveillance may be safe and could reduce unnecessary procedures.
deep_dives.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: Surveillance colonoscopy at 5 years after high-risk adenoma removal is noninferior to surveillance at 3 years regarding 5-year cumulative colorectal cancer incidence.

- Study type: Ongoing randomized noninferiority trial
- Population/setting: 10,799 patients with high-risk adenomas from eight European countries
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: First surveillance colonoscopy at 5 years vs. at 3 years after polyp removal (with the 3-year group also receiving colonoscopy at 5 years)
- Primary endpoints: Cumulative incidence of colorectal cancer at 10 years (interim analysis at 5.5 years)
- Key results: 5-year cumulative colorectal cancer incidence was 0.77% in the 5-year group and 0.82% in the 3-year group (difference, -0.05 percentage points; upper 99.12% CI boundary 0.68, meeting noninferiority); 5 deaths from colorectal cancer occurred (3 in 5-year group, 2 in 3-year group).
- Limitations:
- Interim analysis with only 5.5 years of follow-up; final 10-year results pending
- Potential for missing data due to nonparticipation in surveillance colonoscopy
- Why this matters: These findings support extending the interval for surveillance colonoscopy to 5 years after high-risk adenoma removal, potentially reducing unnecessary procedures without increasing colorectal cancer risk.
deep_dives.journal: The New England journal of medicine
deep_dives.title: Colonoscopy Intervals and Colorectal Cancer Incidence after Adenoma Removal.

cybermed_stored_deep_dive.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: Electromyographic monitoring of the abductor digiti minimi (ADM) and adductor pollicis (AP) muscles provides equivalent results for neuromuscular block onset and recovery, except that ADM recovers faster than AP when monitored on the dominant (right) hand.

- Study type: Prospective, randomized trial
- Population/setting: 44 consenting patients undergoing general anesthesia with simultaneous EMG monitoring of ADM and AP muscles
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: EMG monitoring of ADM muscle versus AP muscle during rocuronium-induced neuromuscular block and sugammadex-induced recovery
- Primary endpoints: Onset time of neuromuscular block (rocuronium to TOF count=0), recovery time (sugammadex to TOF ratio ≥0.9), and time to maximal recovery (sugammadex to TOF ratio=1.0)
- Key results: No significant differences in onset or recovery times between ADM and AP overall; when monitored on the right hand, ADM recovered 93 s (25%) faster to TOF ≥0.9 and 105 s (20%) faster to TOF=1.0 than AP; no difference when monitored on the left hand.
- Limitations:
- Small sample size (44 patients)
- Single-center study
- Handedness and arm dominance may affect generalizability
- Why this matters: Findings support the use of either ADM or AP muscle for neuromuscular monitoring, with consideration of arm dominance for accurate recovery assessment.

cybermed_stored_deep_dive.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: A maternal diet high in eggs and peanuts during pregnancy and lactation did not significantly reduce the risk of egg or peanut allergy in infants at 1 year of age compared to a standard diet.

- Study type: Multisite randomized trial
- Population/setting: Pregnant women with unborn children at high risk for allergic disease (at least two biologic family members with medically diagnosed allergic disease) across multiple sites.
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: High egg-peanut diet (≥6 eggs and 60 peanuts per week) versus standard diet (≤3 eggs and 30 peanuts per week) from before 23 weeks' gestation to 4 months postnatally.
- Primary endpoints: IgE-mediated egg or peanut allergy in the infant at 1 year of age.
- Key results: No significant difference in infant allergy rates: 7.8% in the high egg-peanut group vs. 8.4% in the standard-diet group (relative risk 0.93; 95% CI, 0.69 to 1.26; P = 0.65); safety measures were similar between groups.
- Limitations:
- Study limited to infants at high familial risk for allergy.
- Follow-up only until 1 year of age.
- Dietary adherence and allergen exposure outside the study protocol not fully controlled.
- Why this matters: This study provides evidence that increasing maternal intake of eggs and peanuts during pregnancy and lactation does not prevent egg or peanut allergy in high-risk infants, informing dietary recommendations for expectant and breastfeeding mothers.

BOTTOM LINE: Intrauterine instillation of mepivacaine significantly reduced pain and improved tolerability during IUD placement in nulliparous individuals compared to placebo.

- Study type: Multicenter, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial
- Population/setting: Nulliparous individuals aged 18 to 31 years undergoing IUD placement at 11 outpatient clinics in Sweden
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Intrauterine instillation of 10 mL mepivacaine (20 mg/mL) versus 10 mL sodium chloride (placebo) 2 minutes before IUD placement
- Primary endpoints: Clinician-adjusted difference in pain scores during IUD placement measured on a 100-mm visual analog scale
- Key results: Mean pain score was 43.8 mm in the mepivacaine group vs 58.6 mm in the placebo group (mean difference, 14.8 mm; 95% CI, 10.0-19.6; P < .001); tolerable pain was reported by 98.3% in the mepivacaine group vs 91.4% in the placebo group (relative risk, 1.08; NNT, 15).
- Limitations:
- Study limited to nulliparous individuals aged 18-31 years.
- Only IUDs with smaller-diameter placement tubes were included.
- Exclusion of participants with certain conditions may limit generalizability.
- Why this matters: Reducing pain during IUD placement may increase patient satisfaction and support informed contraceptive choices, potentially improving uptake of IUDs among young, nulliparous individuals.

cybermed_stored_deep_dive.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: Surveillance colonoscopy at 5 years after high-risk adenoma removal is noninferior to surveillance at 3 years regarding 5-year cumulative colorectal cancer incidence.

- Study type: Ongoing randomized noninferiority trial
- Population/setting: 10,799 patients with high-risk adenomas from eight European countries
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: First surveillance colonoscopy at 5 years vs. at 3 years after polyp removal (with the 3-year group also receiving colonoscopy at 5 years)
- Primary endpoints: Cumulative incidence of colorectal cancer at 10 years (interim analysis at 5.5 years)
- Key results: 5-year cumulative colorectal cancer incidence was 0.77% in the 5-year group and 0.82% in the 3-year group (difference, -0.05 percentage points; upper 99.12% CI boundary 0.68, meeting noninferiority); 5 deaths from colorectal cancer occurred (3 in 5-year group, 2 in 3-year group).
- Limitations:
- Interim analysis with only 5.5 years of follow-up; final 10-year results pending
- Potential for missing data due to nonparticipation in surveillance colonoscopy
- Why this matters: These findings support extending the interval for surveillance colonoscopy to 5 years after high-risk adenoma removal, potentially reducing unnecessary procedures without increasing colorectal cancer risk.

cybermed_stored_deep_dive.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: Intraoperative remifentanil administration guided by Analgesia Nociception Index monitoring did not reduce postoperative opioid consumption compared to standard hemodynamic-guided administration in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis surgery.

- Study type: Multicenter randomized controlled trial
- Population/setting: Adolescents undergoing idiopathic scoliosis correction surgery at multiple centers between October 2020 and June 2023 (N=244 randomized).
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Remifentanil administration guided by Analgesia Nociception Index (intervention) versus hemodynamic parameters (control).
- Primary endpoints: Postoperative morphine consumption at day 1.
- Key results: Postoperative morphine consumption at day 1 was similar in both groups (median 0.4 [0.3; 0.8] vs 0.4 [0.3; 0.5] mg/kg; median difference -0.005 [-0.10 to 0.09]; P=0.93), though intraoperative remifentanil use was lower in the ANI group (mean difference 9.5 [4 to 15] μg/kg; P<0.001). No differences were observed in secondary outcomes.
- Limitations:
- Long-term outcomes beyond 6 months not reported.
- Potential variability in nonopioid analgesic use.
- Study limited to adolescent idiopathic scoliosis population.
- Why this matters: This study suggests that intraoperative nociception monitoring with ANI does not reduce postoperative opioid needs in adolescent scoliosis surgery, informing perioperative pain management strategies.
cybermed_stored_deep_dive.title: Effects of Intraoperative Nociception Monitoring during Adolescent Idiopathic Scoliosis Correction.

deep_dives.bottom_line: In this large, multicenter randomized trial of adults undergoing major noncardiac surgery, total intravenous anesthesia (TIVA) did not improve days alive and at home at 30 days compared to volatile inhalational anesthesia, indicating no significant difference in recovery or safety outcomes between these anesthetic approaches. This evidence suggests that either technique can be appropriately chosen based on clinician and patient preference without impacting major postoperative recovery metrics.
deep_dives.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: Total intravenous anesthesia (TIVA) did not improve days alive and at home at 30 days compared with volatile inhalational anesthesia in older adults undergoing major noncardiac surgery.

- Study type: Pragmatic, multicenter, open-label randomized clinical trial
- Population/setting: Patients aged 50 years or older scheduled for elective major noncardiac surgery at 49 UK National Health Service hospitals
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Maintenance of general anesthesia with TIVA (propofol infusion) versus volatile-based inhalational agents
- Primary endpoints: Days alive and at home at 30 days
- Key results: Mean days alive and at home at 30 days were similar between groups (22.5 vs 22.4 days; incidence rate ratio, 1.00; 95% CI, 0.99-1.02; adjusted P = .68); no significant differences in secondary outcomes except lower rates of thirst, hoarseness, and nausea/vomiting in the TIVA group; two cases of unintentional awareness under anesthesia occurred in the TIVA group.
- Limitations:
- Open-label design may introduce bias.
- All other perioperative care was at clinician discretion, potentially introducing variability.
- Study conducted in UK NHS hospitals, which may limit generalizability.
- Why this matters: This study informs anesthetic choice for older adults undergoing major noncardiac surgery, showing no difference in key recovery outcomes between TIVA and inhalational anesthesia.
deep_dives.title: Total Intravenous vs Volatile Inhalational Anesthesia for Major Noncardiac Surgery: A Randomized Clinical Trial.

deep_dives.bottom_line: This meta-analysis of eight RCTs (4,807 patients) found no mortality difference between ketamine and etomidate for rapid sequence intubation in critically ill patients, but ketamine was linked to a higher risk of post-induction cardiovascular collapse (with limited evidence certainty), while etomidate increased adrenal insufficiency risk; clinicians should weigh these risks when selecting an induction agent.
deep_dives.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: Ketamine and etomidate do not differ in mortality for rapid sequence intubation in critically ill patients, but ketamine is linked to a higher risk of post-induction cardiovascular collapse.

- Study type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials
- Population/setting: Critically ill patients undergoing emergency tracheal intubation; 8 RCTs with 4,807 patients
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Ketamine versus etomidate as induction agents for rapid sequence intubation
- Primary endpoints: Mortality at the longest follow-up
- Key results: No significant difference in mortality (RR: 0.97, 95% CI: 0.89-1.06, p = 0.51); ketamine associated with higher risk of post-induction cardiovascular collapse (RR: 1.34, 95% CI: 1.16-1.54, p < 0.01); etomidate associated with higher risk of adrenal insufficiency.
- Limitations:
- Limited number of studies for cardiovascular collapse outcome
- Open-label design in included trials
- Heterogeneity in outcome definitions
- Why this matters: This analysis informs clinicians that while survival outcomes are similar, ketamine may increase the risk of cardiovascular collapse and etomidate may increase adrenal insufficiency risk, guiding safer induction agent selection in critically ill patients.
deep_dives.title: Ketamine versus Etomidate as an induction agent for tracheal intubation: An updated meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials.

deep_dives.bottom_line: This methodologic survey found that randomized trials underpinning perioperative anesthesia guidelines often have a low Fragility Index (median FI = 4), indicating that their statistically significant results can be overturned by only a few outcome events; this highlights the need for cautious interpretation of guideline recommendations based on potentially fragile evidence.
deep_dives.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: Randomized superiority trials supporting perioperative anesthesia guidelines are generally small and have modest Fragility Index values, suggesting that their statistical significance often relies on a small number of outcome events.

- Study type: Methodologic survey of randomized controlled trials cited in clinical practice guidelines
- Population/setting: RCTs with binary outcomes in adult, pediatric, obstetric, cardiovascular, and regional anesthesia populations referenced in North American and European perioperative guidelines (2012-2022)
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Methodologic survey of randomized controlled trials cited in clinical practice guidelines
- Primary endpoints: Fragility Index, Reverse Fragility Index, and Fragility Quotient of included RCTs
- Key results: Among 161 superiority trials, the median Fragility Index was 4 (IQR 2 to 8); cardiovascular trials had the highest median FI (6), pediatric trials the lowest (1); obstetric trials had higher FI than adult trials (IRR 1.63), and single-center trials had lower FI than multicenter trials (IRR 0.52).
- Limitations:
- Only RCTs with binary outcomes were included.
- Primary analyses were restricted to superiority trials.
- Exploratory regression analyses may be subject to residual confounding.
- Why this matters: Understanding the fragility of evidence supporting perioperative anesthesia guidelines highlights the need for cautious interpretation and may inform future trial design and guideline development.
deep_dives.title: Fragility Index of Randomized Clinical Trials in Perioperative Anesthesia: A Methodologic Survey of Guideline-supporting Evidence.

deep_dives.bottom_line: Combined analysis of two large phase 3 trials shows that inhaled treprostinil significantly slows lung function decline, delays clinical worsening and exacerbations, and improves quality of life in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis over 52 weeks, providing strong evidence to support its use as a new therapeutic option for IPF.

BOTTOM LINE: Inhaled treprostinil significantly slowed lung function decline and improved multiple clinical outcomes in patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) over 52 weeks.

- Study type: Two replicate phase 3 double-blind randomized controlled trials with integrated analysis
- Population/setting: 1191 patients with IPF randomized across two multicenter trials (TETON-1 and TETON-2)
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Inhaled treprostinil versus placebo
- Primary endpoints: Change in absolute forced vital capacity (FVC) at week 52
- Key results: Median FVC change at 52 weeks was -45.4 ml with treprostinil vs -161.7 ml with placebo (between-group difference 111.8 ml, 95% CI 79.7 to 144.0, p < 0.0001); treprostinil was superior in five of six secondary endpoints, including time to clinical worsening, time to IPF exacerbation, quality of life, ppDLCO, and ppFVC; mortality was 6.9% with treprostinil vs 9.4% with placebo.
- Limitations:
- Long-term safety and efficacy beyond 52 weeks not assessed
- Cough was the most common adverse event
- Results may not generalize to all IPF populations
- Why this matters: These findings support inhaled treprostinil as an effective treatment option to slow disease progression and improve outcomes in patients with IPF.

deep_dives.bottom_line: In this randomized, blinded trial of high-risk adults undergoing major noncardiac surgery, a preoperative intravenous crystalloid bolus did not significantly reduce postinduction hypotension compared to standard care, indicating that routine pre-induction fluid bolusing may not be effective for preventing hypotension in this population.
deep_dives.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: Preoperative intravenous crystalloid bolus does not significantly reduce postinduction hypotension in high-risk patients undergoing major noncardiac surgery.

- Study type: Prospective, randomized, single-blind clinical trial
- Population/setting: Adult patients aged 45 years or older with cardiovascular risk factors undergoing major noncardiac elective surgery at two centers in Austria (Medical University of Graz and Medical University of Vienna); N=504 analyzed.
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Preoperative intravenous crystalloid bolus (500–1,000 ml within 60 ± 15 min before induction) versus standard care (no additional preoperative bolus).
- Primary endpoints: Time-weighted average mean arterial pressure (MAP) less than 65 mmHg within the first 20 min after induction or until surgical incision.
- Key results: No statistically significant difference in median time-weighted average MAP <65 mmHg between groups (intervention: 0.0 mmHg [IQR 0.0–0.56] vs. standard care: 0.0 mmHg [IQR 0.0–0.84]; P=0.368); no significant differences in vasopressor use or time to first MAP <65 mmHg.
- Limitations:
- Single-blind design (anesthesiologists blinded, but not patients or study personnel administering fluids).
- Anesthetic management and intraoperative care were not standardized.
- Secondary hemodynamic endpoints (e.g., cardiac output) only measured at one site.
- Study may not be generalizable to other populations or surgical settings.
- Why this matters: Routine preoperative crystalloid fluid bolus does not prevent postinduction hypotension in high-risk surgical patients, suggesting such practice may not improve perioperative hemodynamic outcomes.
deep_dives.title: Effect of Preoperative Intravenous Crystalloid Bolus on Postinduction Blood Pressure: A Randomized Blinded Intervention Trial.

cybermed_stored_deep_dive.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: Total intravenous anesthesia (TIVA) did not improve days alive and at home at 30 days compared with volatile inhalational anesthesia in older adults undergoing major noncardiac surgery.

- Study type: Pragmatic, multicenter, open-label randomized clinical trial
- Population/setting: Patients aged 50 years or older scheduled for elective major noncardiac surgery at 49 UK National Health Service hospitals
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Maintenance of general anesthesia with TIVA (propofol infusion) versus volatile-based inhalational agents
- Primary endpoints: Days alive and at home at 30 days
- Key results: Mean days alive and at home at 30 days were similar between groups (22.5 vs 22.4 days; incidence rate ratio, 1.00; 95% CI, 0.99-1.02; adjusted P = .68); no significant differences in secondary outcomes except lower rates of thirst, hoarseness, and nausea/vomiting in the TIVA group; two cases of unintentional awareness under anesthesia occurred in the TIVA group.
- Limitations:
- Open-label design may introduce bias.
- All other perioperative care was at clinician discretion, potentially introducing variability.
- Study conducted in UK NHS hospitals, which may limit generalizability.
- Why this matters: This study informs anesthetic choice for older adults undergoing major noncardiac surgery, showing no difference in key recovery outcomes between TIVA and inhalational anesthesia.
cybermed_stored_deep_dive.title: Total Intravenous vs Volatile Inhalational Anesthesia for Major Noncardiac Surgery: A Randomized Clinical Trial.

cybermed_stored_deep_dive.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: Ketamine and etomidate do not differ in mortality for rapid sequence intubation in critically ill patients, but ketamine is linked to a higher risk of post-induction cardiovascular collapse.

- Study type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials
- Population/setting: Critically ill patients undergoing emergency tracheal intubation; 8 RCTs with 4,807 patients
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Ketamine versus etomidate as induction agents for rapid sequence intubation
- Primary endpoints: Mortality at the longest follow-up
- Key results: No significant difference in mortality (RR: 0.97, 95% CI: 0.89-1.06, p = 0.51); ketamine associated with higher risk of post-induction cardiovascular collapse (RR: 1.34, 95% CI: 1.16-1.54, p < 0.01); etomidate associated with higher risk of adrenal insufficiency.
- Limitations:
- Limited number of studies for cardiovascular collapse outcome
- Open-label design in included trials
- Heterogeneity in outcome definitions
- Why this matters: This analysis informs clinicians that while survival outcomes are similar, ketamine may increase the risk of cardiovascular collapse and etomidate may increase adrenal insufficiency risk, guiding safer induction agent selection in critically ill patients.

BOTTOM LINE: Inhaled treprostinil significantly slowed lung function decline and improved multiple clinical outcomes in patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) over 52 weeks.

- Study type: Two replicate phase 3 double-blind randomized controlled trials with integrated analysis
- Population/setting: 1191 patients with IPF randomized across two multicenter trials (TETON-1 and TETON-2)
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Inhaled treprostinil versus placebo
- Primary endpoints: Change in absolute forced vital capacity (FVC) at week 52
- Key results: Median FVC change at 52 weeks was -45.4 ml with treprostinil vs -161.7 ml with placebo (between-group difference 111.8 ml, 95% CI 79.7 to 144.0, p < 0.0001); treprostinil was superior in five of six secondary endpoints, including time to clinical worsening, time to IPF exacerbation, quality of life, ppDLCO, and ppFVC; mortality was 6.9% with treprostinil vs 9.4% with placebo.
- Limitations:
- Long-term safety and efficacy beyond 52 weeks not assessed
- Cough was the most common adverse event
- Results may not generalize to all IPF populations
- Why this matters: These findings support inhaled treprostinil as an effective treatment option to slow disease progression and improve outcomes in patients with IPF.

cybermed_stored_deep_dive.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: Preoperative intravenous crystalloid bolus does not significantly reduce postinduction hypotension in high-risk patients undergoing major noncardiac surgery.

- Study type: Prospective, randomized, single-blind clinical trial
- Population/setting: Adult patients aged 45 years or older with cardiovascular risk factors undergoing major noncardiac elective surgery at two centers in Austria (Medical University of Graz and Medical University of Vienna); N=504 analyzed.
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Preoperative intravenous crystalloid bolus (500–1,000 ml within 60 ± 15 min before induction) versus standard care (no additional preoperative bolus).
- Primary endpoints: Time-weighted average mean arterial pressure (MAP) less than 65 mmHg within the first 20 min after induction or until surgical incision.
- Key results: No statistically significant difference in median time-weighted average MAP <65 mmHg between groups (intervention: 0.0 mmHg [IQR 0.0–0.56] vs. standard care: 0.0 mmHg [IQR 0.0–0.84]; P=0.368); no significant differences in vasopressor use or time to first MAP <65 mmHg.
- Limitations:
- Single-blind design (anesthesiologists blinded, but not patients or study personnel administering fluids).
- Anesthetic management and intraoperative care were not standardized.
- Secondary hemodynamic endpoints (e.g., cardiac output) only measured at one site.
- Study may not be generalizable to other populations or surgical settings.
- Why this matters: Routine preoperative crystalloid fluid bolus does not prevent postinduction hypotension in high-risk surgical patients, suggesting such practice may not improve perioperative hemodynamic outcomes.

deep_dives.bottom_line: This cross-sectional analysis found that over 90% of randomized controlled trials of regional anesthesia registered on ClinicalTrials.gov had substantive, undisclosed changes to outcome measures between registry versions, often occurring after trial completion or publication; this highlights significant concerns about transparency and potential bias in outcome reporting, which may impact the interpretation and reliability of RA trial evidence.
deep_dives.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: Substantive changes to prespecified outcomes in regional anesthesia randomized trials are common, often occur after trial completion or publication, and are rarely disclosed.

- Study type: Registry-based cross-sectional analysis
- Population/setting: 74 interventional regional anesthesia trials enrolling adults, registered on ClinicalTrials.gov between January 2017 and December 2024, with posted results and linked peer-reviewed publications.
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Comparison of earliest and most recent registry records for outcome definitions, timing, and classifications.
- Primary endpoints: Frequency, type, timing, and disclosure of modifications to prespecified outcomes in trial registries and publications.
- Key results: 91.9% of trials had at least one substantive outcome change; 47.1% of substantive modifications occurred after primary completion and 51.5% after publication, with none disclosed; 37.8% had high-impact modifications, and secondary outcomes were more frequently added or removed than primary outcomes.
- Limitations:
- Cannot determine reasons for outcome changes.
- Cannot assess whether changes influenced reported results.
- Limited to trials registered on ClinicalTrials.gov with posted results and linked publications.
- Why this matters: Frequent and undisclosed changes to trial outcomes may undermine transparency and trust in published evidence for regional anesthesia interventions.
deep_dives.title: Assessing the changes in outcome measurements in randomized controlled trials of regional anesthesia interventions: a registry-publication comparison study.

deep_dives.bottom_line: This sub-study of the randomized, placebo-controlled INBUILD trial (N=474) shows that quantitative CT measurements predict disease progression and mortality in progressive pulmonary fibrosis and are sensitive to treatment effects of nintedanib, supporting their use as prognostic and efficacy biomarkers in clinical trials.
deep_dives.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: Quantitative CT measurements can predict disease progression and assess treatment efficacy in patients with progressive pulmonary fibrosis.

- Study type: Sub-study of a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial
- Population/setting: Patients with progressive pulmonary fibrosis (N = 474) from the INBUILD trial
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Nintedanib versus placebo; quantitative CT measurements using UCLA and e-Lung algorithms
- Primary endpoints: Associations between quantitative CT scores and ILD progression; effect of nintedanib on quantitative CT measurements
- Key results: Higher baseline QCT scores predicted greater FVC decline and higher risk of FVC % predicted decline ≥10% or death over 52 weeks; nintedanib significantly reduced QILD score and e-Lung TDE at weeks 24 and 52 compared to placebo (relative difference ~-7% to -8%, p ≤ 0.005).
- Limitations:
- Sub-study design may limit generalizability.
- Details on patient selection and algorithm performance not fully described.
- Why this matters: Quantitative CT can enhance prognostication and monitoring of treatment response in clinical trials for progressive pulmonary fibrosis.

deep_dives.bottom_line: In this small, single-center crossover trial of ventilated ARDS patients, intravenous ondansetron significantly reduced respiratory drive and effort, suggesting potential to facilitate safer spontaneous ventilation and reduce the need for deep sedation or neuromuscular blockade, though larger studies are needed to confirm these findings.
deep_dives.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: Ondansetron reduces respiratory drive in invasively mechanically ventilated patients with ARDS.

- Study type: Single-center, single-blind, non-randomized crossover trial
- Population/setting: Nine adult patients with ARDS (Berlin criteria), ventilated >48 hours, on pressure-support mode, in a single center
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Intravenous ondansetron (0.15 mg/kg; max 16 mg) versus intravenous placebo (10 mL 0.9% saline)
- Primary endpoints: Pressure-time-product (PTP) of esophageal pressure (Peso) per minute; respiratory rate, tidal volume, minute ventilation, and electrical activity of the diaphragm (Edi)
- Key results: Ondansetron reduced mean inspiratory PTP by -23 cmH2O·s·min-1 (95% CI [-28, -18]; p<0.001), respiratory rate by -1.7 breaths/min (95% CI [-2.0, -1.3]), minute ventilation by -1.0 L/min (95% CI [-1.1, -0.8]), and peak Edi by -2.4 μV (95% CI [-2.6, -2.2]); PaCO2 rose by +3.2 mmHg (95% CI [+1.4, +5.1]; p<0.001) and PaO2:FiO2 improved by +23 (95% CI [6, 40]; p=0.009); tidal volume did not change significantly.
- Limitations:
- Small sample size (n=9)
- Single-center design
- Non-randomized and single-blind
- Short-term physiological endpoints only
- Why this matters: Reducing respiratory drive with ondansetron may enable safer spontaneous ventilation in ARDS patients, potentially reducing the need for deep sedation or neuromuscular blockade.
deep_dives.title: Effect of ondansetron on respiratory drive in patients with acute respiratory distress syndrome.

deep_dives.bottom_line: This post hoc Bayesian analysis of the AID-ICU trial suggests that haloperidol may provide moderate to high probabilities of benefit for both hypoactive and hyperactive delirium in ICU patients, with a moderate probability of greater benefit in hyperactive delirium; however, the evidence is not definitive and further research is needed to confirm these findings, which could influence delirium management strategies in critical care.
deep_dives.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: Haloperidol was associated with moderate to high probabilities of benefit for both hypoactive and hyperactive delirium in ICU patients, with a tendency toward greater effects in hyperactive delirium.

- Study type: Post hoc Bayesian analysis of a randomized controlled trial
- Population/setting: Adult ICU patients with delirium (N=987) from the AID-ICU trial
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Haloperidol versus placebo
- Primary endpoints: Days alive out of hospital at 90 days, days alive without delirium/coma, days alive without mechanical ventilation, and mortality
- Key results: Haloperidol was associated with more days alive out of hospital in both subgroups, with a 76.5% probability of greater benefit in hyperactive delirium (difference in mean days 2.9; 95% CrI -4.8 to 10.6); similar trends were seen for other endpoints, and there were no relevant differences in serious adverse reactions or rescue medication use.
- Limitations:
- Post hoc analysis
- Probabilities rather than definitive statistical significance
- Confidence intervals include the possibility of no effect
- Further research is needed to confirm findings
