cybermed_stored_deep_dive.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: Substantive changes to prespecified outcomes in regional anesthesia randomized trials are common, often occur after trial completion or publication, and are rarely disclosed.

- Study type: Registry-based cross-sectional analysis
- Population/setting: 74 interventional regional anesthesia trials enrolling adults, registered on ClinicalTrials.gov between January 2017 and December 2024, with posted results and linked peer-reviewed publications.
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Comparison of earliest and most recent registry records for outcome definitions, timing, and classifications.
- Primary endpoints: Frequency, type, timing, and disclosure of modifications to prespecified outcomes in trial registries and publications.
- Key results: 91.9% of trials had at least one substantive outcome change; 47.1% of substantive modifications occurred after primary completion and 51.5% after publication, with none disclosed; 37.8% had high-impact modifications, and secondary outcomes were more frequently added or removed than primary outcomes.
- Limitations:
- Cannot determine reasons for outcome changes.
- Cannot assess whether changes influenced reported results.
- Limited to trials registered on ClinicalTrials.gov with posted results and linked publications.
- Why this matters: Frequent and undisclosed changes to trial outcomes may undermine transparency and trust in published evidence for regional anesthesia interventions.
cybermed_stored_deep_dive.title: Assessing the changes in outcome measurements in randomized controlled trials of regional anesthesia interventions: a registry-publication comparison study.

cybermed_stored_deep_dive.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: Quantitative CT measurements can predict disease progression and assess treatment efficacy in patients with progressive pulmonary fibrosis.

- Study type: Sub-study of a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial
- Population/setting: Patients with progressive pulmonary fibrosis (N = 474) from the INBUILD trial
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Nintedanib versus placebo; quantitative CT measurements using UCLA and e-Lung algorithms
- Primary endpoints: Associations between quantitative CT scores and ILD progression; effect of nintedanib on quantitative CT measurements
- Key results: Higher baseline QCT scores predicted greater FVC decline and higher risk of FVC % predicted decline ≥10% or death over 52 weeks; nintedanib significantly reduced QILD score and e-Lung TDE at weeks 24 and 52 compared to placebo (relative difference ~-7% to -8%, p ≤ 0.005).
- Limitations:
- Sub-study design may limit generalizability.
- Details on patient selection and algorithm performance not fully described.
- Why this matters: Quantitative CT can enhance prognostication and monitoring of treatment response in clinical trials for progressive pulmonary fibrosis.

cybermed_stored_deep_dive.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: Ondansetron reduces respiratory drive in invasively mechanically ventilated patients with ARDS.

- Study type: Single-center, single-blind, non-randomized crossover trial
- Population/setting: Nine adult patients with ARDS (Berlin criteria), ventilated >48 hours, on pressure-support mode, in a single center
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Intravenous ondansetron (0.15 mg/kg; max 16 mg) versus intravenous placebo (10 mL 0.9% saline)
- Primary endpoints: Pressure-time-product (PTP) of esophageal pressure (Peso) per minute; respiratory rate, tidal volume, minute ventilation, and electrical activity of the diaphragm (Edi)
- Key results: Ondansetron reduced mean inspiratory PTP by -23 cmH2O·s·min-1 (95% CI [-28, -18]; p<0.001), respiratory rate by -1.7 breaths/min (95% CI [-2.0, -1.3]), minute ventilation by -1.0 L/min (95% CI [-1.1, -0.8]), and peak Edi by -2.4 μV (95% CI [-2.6, -2.2]); PaCO2 rose by +3.2 mmHg (95% CI [+1.4, +5.1]; p<0.001) and PaO2:FiO2 improved by +23 (95% CI [6, 40]; p=0.009); tidal volume did not change significantly.
- Limitations:
- Small sample size (n=9)
- Single-center design
- Non-randomized and single-blind
- Short-term physiological endpoints only
- Why this matters: Reducing respiratory drive with ondansetron may enable safer spontaneous ventilation in ARDS patients, potentially reducing the need for deep sedation or neuromuscular blockade.

BOTTOM LINE: Ondansetron reduces respiratory drive in invasively mechanically ventilated patients with ARDS.

- Study type: Single-center, single-blind, non-randomized crossover trial
- Population/setting: Nine adult patients with ARDS (Berlin criteria), ventilated >48 hours, on pressure-support mode, in a single center
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Intravenous ondansetron (0.15 mg/kg; max 16 mg) versus intravenous placebo (10 mL 0.9% saline)
- Primary endpoints: Pressure-time-product (PTP) of esophageal pressure (Peso) per minute; respiratory rate, tidal volume, minute ventilation, and electrical activity of the diaphragm (Edi)
- Key results: Ondansetron reduced mean inspiratory PTP by -23 cmH2O·s·min-1 (95% CI [-28, -18]; p<0.001), respiratory rate by -1.7 breaths/min (95% CI [-2.0, -1.3]), minute ventilation by -1.0 L/min (95% CI [-1.1, -0.8]), and peak Edi by -2.4 μV (95% CI [-2.6, -2.2]); PaCO2 rose by +3.2 mmHg (95% CI [+1.4, +5.1]; p<0.001) and PaO2:FiO2 improved by +23 (95% CI [6, 40]; p=0.009); tidal volume did not change significantly.
- Limitations:
- Small sample size (n=9)
- Single-center design
- Non-randomized and single-blind
- Short-term physiological endpoints only
- Why this matters: Reducing respiratory drive with ondansetron may enable safer spontaneous ventilation in ARDS patients, potentially reducing the need for deep sedation or neuromuscular blockade.

cybermed_stored_deep_dive.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: Haloperidol was associated with moderate to high probabilities of benefit for both hypoactive and hyperactive delirium in ICU patients, with a tendency toward greater effects in hyperactive delirium.

- Study type: Post hoc Bayesian analysis of a randomized controlled trial
- Population/setting: Adult ICU patients with delirium (N=987) from the AID-ICU trial
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Haloperidol versus placebo
- Primary endpoints: Days alive out of hospital at 90 days, days alive without delirium/coma, days alive without mechanical ventilation, and mortality
- Key results: Haloperidol was associated with more days alive out of hospital in both subgroups, with a 76.5% probability of greater benefit in hyperactive delirium (difference in mean days 2.9; 95% CrI -4.8 to 10.6); similar trends were seen for other endpoints, and there were no relevant differences in serious adverse reactions or rescue medication use.
- Limitations:
- Post hoc analysis
- Probabilities rather than definitive statistical significance
- Confidence intervals include the possibility of no effect
- Further research is needed to confirm findings
- Why this matters: Understanding differential effects of haloperidol by delirium subtype may help tailor treatment strategies for ICU patients with delirium.
cybermed_stored_deep_dive.title: Haloperidol for Hypoactive and Hyperactive Delirium in ICU Patients-A Post Hoc Bayesian Analysis of the AID-ICU Trial.

Clinicians should interpret guideline recommendations with caution, recognizing the potential instability of the underlying trial data.

deep_dives.bottom_line: Expanding lung cancer LDCT screening eligibility beyond smokers, as seen in China, increases early-stage detection but lacks strong evidence for mortality benefit and may heighten overdiagnosis; clinical decisions for non-smokers should be guided by prospective data showing reduced advanced-stage incidence rather than stage shift alone.
deep_dives.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: Expanding lung cancer LDCT screening eligibility beyond smoking-based criteria, especially in China, requires prospective evidence of reduced advanced-stage incidence, as current data suggest potential for increased overdiagnosis without clear mortality benefit.

- Study type: Narrative review
- Population/setting: Populations with and without substantial smoking history, with a focus on Chinese lung cancer screening programs
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: LDCT screening in populations with substantial tobacco exposure versus populations without substantial smoking history
- Primary endpoints: Reduction in advanced-stage lung cancer incidence and lung cancer mortality
- Key results: LDCT screening can increase early-stage detection but may not reduce advanced-stage incidence or mortality in populations without substantial smoking history; recent data from China and South Korea indicate increased overdiagnosis when LDCT is used in average-risk populations.
- Limitations:
- Not an exhaustive systematic review
- Relies on interpretation of existing studies rather than new primary data
- Potential for bias in narrative synthesis
- Why this matters: Guidelines for lung cancer screening eligibility should be based on prospective evidence of mortality or advanced-stage incidence reduction, particularly in never- or light-smoker populations, to avoid harms from overdiagnosis.
deep_dives.title: Lung Cancer Screening Beyond Smoking-Based Eligibility: Evidence, Limits, and Lessons From China.

deep_dives.bottom_line: A newly derived and validated claims-based algorithm combining diagnostic codes with treatment-based criteria accurately identifies cardiogenic shock (sensitivity 0.89–0.95, specificity 0.90), enabling robust large-scale epidemiologic and outcomes research using administrative data. This facilitates improved surveillance and research on cardiogenic shock in real-world populations.
deep_dives.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: A claims-based algorithm combining diagnostic codes and treatment-based criteria accurately identifies cardiogenic shock in administrative data, enabling reliable large-scale research and outcome assessment.

- Study type: Diagnostic accuracy study
- Population/setting: Patients from a single-center cardiac ICU registry (n=10,156), a multicenter cardiogenic shock registry (RESCUE, n=1,247), and a nationwide Korean administrative claims database (n=207,419).
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Claims-based operational definition for cardiogenic shock versus clinically adjudicated reference standards.
- Primary endpoints: Diagnostic accuracy (sensitivity, specificity, overall accuracy) of the claims-based algorithm for identifying cardiogenic shock.
- Key results: In the CICU cohort, sensitivity was 0.89, specificity 0.90, and overall accuracy 0.90; in the RESCUE cohort, sensitivity was 0.95; nationwide, 207,419 patients with cardiogenic shock were identified, with cumulative mortality rates of 37.9% at 12 months, 49.9% at 5 years, and 61.7% at 10 years.
- Limitations:
- Validation limited to Korean cohorts and administrative data.
- Potential misclassification due to reliance on coding and treatment criteria.
- No external validation in non-Korean populations.
- Why this matters: This validated claims-based definition allows for robust epidemiologic and outcome studies of cardiogenic shock using large administrative datasets, supporting system-level evaluation and quality improvement in critical care.
deep_dives.title: Derivation and Validation of Operational Definitions From Claims Data for Identifying Cardiogenic Shock.

deep_dives.bottom_line: This secondary analysis of the ACORN trial shows that individual patient characteristics can predict differential benefit from cefepime versus piperacillin-tazobactam regarding survival without acute kidney injury, suggesting that personalized antibiotic selection may improve outcomes in hospitalized adults with acute infection. The evidence is moderate and clinically relevant for tailoring empiric antibiotic therapy to reduce kidney injury risk.
deep_dives.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: Individual patient characteristics influence the effect of cefepime versus piperacillin-tazobactam on survival without acute kidney injury in adults hospitalized with acute infection.

- Study type: Secondary analysis of a randomized controlled trial
- Population/setting: Adults hospitalized with acute infection in the ACORN trial
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Cefepime versus piperacillin-tazobactam
- Primary endpoints: Survival without acute kidney injury; secondary endpoint: survival without delirium or coma
- Key results: Among patients predicted to benefit from cefepime, 81.2% survived without acute kidney injury versus 74.2% with piperacillin-tazobactam (difference 7.1%; 95% CI, 0.25 to 13.9%); among those predicted to benefit from piperacillin-tazobactam, 56.6% survived without acute kidney injury on cefepime versus 63.0% on piperacillin-tazobactam (difference -6.3%; 95% CI, -20.7 to 8.2%). Individual characteristics did not modify the effect on survival without delirium or coma.
- Limitations:
- Secondary analysis rather than a primary randomized comparison
- Effect model validation limited to the trial cohort
- Potential unmeasured confounding
- Why this matters: Personalizing antibiotic choice based on individual patient characteristics may improve outcomes related to acute kidney injury in hospitalized adults with acute infection.
deep_dives.journal: American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine
deep_dives.title: Individualized Treatment Effects of Cefepime vs Piperacillin-Tazobactam in Adults Hospitalized with Acute Infection.

deep_dives.bottom_line: This multicenter randomized trial found no significant difference in urethrocutaneous fistula rates after hypospadias repair in children under 2 years when comparing caudal versus penile block, though caudal block reduced perioperative opioid use and pain scores; however, early termination and limited follow-up mean clinically important differences cannot be ruled out, so results should be interpreted with caution.
deep_dives.deep_dive_markdown:
**BOTTOM LINE:** This multicenter randomized trial found no significant difference in urethrocutaneous fistula rates after hypospadias repair in children under 2 years when comparing caudal versus penile block, though caudal block reduced perioperative opioid use and pain scores; however, early termination and limited follow-up mean clinically important differences cannot be ruled out, so results should be interpreted with caution.

BOTTOM LINE: Caudal and penile blocks showed no significant difference in urethrocutaneous fistula formation after hypospadias repair in children under 2 years, but caudal block reduced perioperative opioid use and pain scores.

- Study type: Multicenter randomized, non-inferiority trial
- Population/setting: Children ≤2 years undergoing primary single-stage midshaft or distal hypospadias repair at 16 Pediatric Regional Anesthesia Network centers
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Caudal block versus penile block, both with general anesthesia
- Primary endpoints: Urethrocutaneous fistula (UCF) formation within 3 postoperative months
- Key results: UCF occurred in 8.9% (7/79) of caudal block and 7.3% (6/82) of penile block patients (RR=0.98; 95% CI 0.35–2.76; p=0.9); caudal block group received less intraoperative (33% vs 56%, p<0.001) and rescue opioids (4.9% vs 15.7%, p=0.01), and had lower mean PACU FLACC pain scores (0.49±1.34 vs 1.14±2.3, p=0.03).
- Limitations:
- Incomplete enrollment
- Loss to follow-up
- Wide confidence intervals limit precision
- Early trial termination
- Clinically important differences cannot be excluded
- Why this matters: This study provides prospective evidence to inform anesthetic choice in pediatric hypospadias repair, suggesting caudal block may reduce opioid use and pain without increasing fistula risk.
deep_dives.title: Caudal versus penile block and urethrocutaneous fistula formation following hypospadias repair in children <2 years: a multicenter randomized clinical trial.

deep_dives.bottom_line: Three randomized trials in low-resource settings found that maternal nutritional supplementation during lactation increased B-vitamin content in human milk but did not alter macronutrients or other major milk components, and postnatal supplementation improved infant growth only among the most undernourished; these findings support extending maternal supplementation into lactation to enhance milk micronutrient quality.
deep_dives.deep_dive_markdown:
**BOTTOM LINE:** Three randomized trials in low-resource settings found that maternal nutritional supplementation during lactation increased B-vitamin content in human milk but did not alter macronutrients or other major milk components, and postnatal supplementation improved infant growth only among the most undernourished; these findings support extending maternal supplementation into lactation to enhance milk micronutrient quality.

BOTTOM LINE: Maternal nutritional supplementation during lactation increases B-vitamin content in human milk, with limited effects on other milk components, and may improve infant growth in undernourished populations.

- Study type: Harmonized analysis of three randomized controlled trials
- Population/setting: Lactating mothers and their infants in Burkina Faso (MISAME-III), Pakistan (Mumta-LW), and Tanzania (ELICIT)
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Maternal balanced energy-protein (BEP) supplements or nicotinamide versus standard care/placebo
- Primary endpoints: Changes in human milk composition (B-vitamins, macronutrients, oligosaccharides, bioactive proteins, microbiome), and infant growth
- Key results: BEP or nicotinamide supplementation increased milk B-vitamin levels; other milk components were largely unchanged; postnatal BEP improved infant growth only in the more undernourished cohort; maternal and infant blood showed concordant changes in a subset.
- Limitations:
- Limited to three low-resource settings
- Infant growth benefit observed only in the most undernourished cohort
- Not all milk components were affected by supplementation
- Why this matters: Extending maternal supplementation into lactation can improve milk micronutrient quality and may benefit infant growth in populations at risk of undernutrition.
deep_dives.title: Nutritional interventions' impacts on human milk: Three trials in low-resource settings.

cybermed_stored_deep_dive.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: Expanding lung cancer LDCT screening eligibility beyond smoking-based criteria, especially in China, requires prospective evidence of reduced advanced-stage incidence, as current data suggest potential for increased overdiagnosis without clear mortality benefit.

- Study type: Narrative review
- Population/setting: Populations with and without substantial smoking history, with a focus on Chinese lung cancer screening programs
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: LDCT screening in populations with substantial tobacco exposure versus populations without substantial smoking history
- Primary endpoints: Reduction in advanced-stage lung cancer incidence and lung cancer mortality
- Key results: LDCT screening can increase early-stage detection but may not reduce advanced-stage incidence or mortality in populations without substantial smoking history; recent data from China and South Korea indicate increased overdiagnosis when LDCT is used in average-risk populations.
- Limitations:
- Not an exhaustive systematic review
- Relies on interpretation of existing studies rather than new primary data
- Potential for bias in narrative synthesis
- Why this matters: Guidelines for lung cancer screening eligibility should be based on prospective evidence of mortality or advanced-stage incidence reduction, particularly in never- or light-smoker populations, to avoid harms from overdiagnosis.

cybermed_stored_deep_dive.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: A claims-based algorithm combining diagnostic codes and treatment-based criteria accurately identifies cardiogenic shock in administrative data, enabling reliable large-scale research and outcome assessment.

- Study type: Diagnostic accuracy study
- Population/setting: Patients from a single-center cardiac ICU registry (n=10,156), a multicenter cardiogenic shock registry (RESCUE, n=1,247), and a nationwide Korean administrative claims database (n=207,419).
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Claims-based operational definition for cardiogenic shock versus clinically adjudicated reference standards.
- Primary endpoints: Diagnostic accuracy (sensitivity, specificity, overall accuracy) of the claims-based algorithm for identifying cardiogenic shock.
- Key results: In the CICU cohort, sensitivity was 0.89, specificity 0.90, and overall accuracy 0.90; in the RESCUE cohort, sensitivity was 0.95; nationwide, 207,419 patients with cardiogenic shock were identified, with cumulative mortality rates of 37.9% at 12 months, 49.9% at 5 years, and 61.7% at 10 years.
- Limitations:
- Validation limited to Korean cohorts and administrative data.
- Potential misclassification due to reliance on coding and treatment criteria.
- No external validation in non-Korean populations.
- Why this matters: This validated claims-based definition allows for robust epidemiologic and outcome studies of cardiogenic shock using large administrative datasets, supporting system-level evaluation and quality improvement in critical care.

cybermed_stored_deep_dive.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: Individual patient characteristics influence the effect of cefepime versus piperacillin-tazobactam on survival without acute kidney injury in adults hospitalized with acute infection.

- Study type: Secondary analysis of a randomized controlled trial
- Population/setting: Adults hospitalized with acute infection in the ACORN trial
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Cefepime versus piperacillin-tazobactam
- Primary endpoints: Survival without acute kidney injury; secondary endpoint: survival without delirium or coma
- Key results: Among patients predicted to benefit from cefepime, 81.2% survived without acute kidney injury versus 74.2% with piperacillin-tazobactam (difference 7.1%; 95% CI, 0.25 to 13.9%); among those predicted to benefit from piperacillin-tazobactam, 56.6% survived without acute kidney injury on cefepime versus 63.0% on piperacillin-tazobactam (difference -6.3%; 95% CI, -20.7 to 8.2%). Individual characteristics did not modify the effect on survival without delirium or coma.
- Limitations:
- Secondary analysis rather than a primary randomized comparison
- Effect model validation limited to the trial cohort
- Potential unmeasured confounding
- Why this matters: Personalizing antibiotic choice based on individual patient characteristics may improve outcomes related to acute kidney injury in hospitalized adults with acute infection.

BOTTOM LINE: Caudal and penile blocks showed no significant difference in urethrocutaneous fistula formation after hypospadias repair in children under 2 years, but caudal block reduced perioperative opioid use and pain scores.

- Study type: Multicenter randomized, non-inferiority trial
- Population/setting: Children ≤2 years undergoing primary single-stage midshaft or distal hypospadias repair at 16 Pediatric Regional Anesthesia Network centers
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Caudal block versus penile block, both with general anesthesia
- Primary endpoints: Urethrocutaneous fistula (UCF) formation within 3 postoperative months
- Key results: UCF occurred in 8.9% (7/79) of caudal block and 7.3% (6/82) of penile block patients (RR=0.98; 95% CI 0.35–2.76; p=0.9); caudal block group received less intraoperative (33% vs 56%, p<0.001) and rescue opioids (4.9% vs 15.7%, p=0.01), and had lower mean PACU FLACC pain scores (0.49±1.34 vs 1.14±2.3, p=0.03).
- Limitations:
- Incomplete enrollment
- Loss to follow-up
- Wide confidence intervals limit precision
- Early trial termination
- Clinically important differences cannot be excluded
- Why this matters: This study provides prospective evidence to inform anesthetic choice in pediatric hypospadias repair, suggesting caudal block may reduce opioid use and pain without increasing fistula risk.
cybermed_stored_deep_dive.title: Caudal versus penile block and urethrocutaneous fistula formation following hypospadias repair in children <2 years: a multicenter randomized clinical trial.

BOTTOM LINE: Caudal and penile blocks showed no significant difference in urethrocutaneous fistula formation after hypospadias repair in children under 2 years, but caudal block reduced perioperative opioid use and pain scores.

- Study type: Multicenter randomized, non-inferiority trial
- Population/setting: Children ≤2 years undergoing primary single-stage midshaft or distal hypospadias repair at 16 Pediatric Regional Anesthesia Network centers
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Caudal block versus penile block, both with general anesthesia
- Primary endpoints: Urethrocutaneous fistula (UCF) formation within 3 postoperative months
- Key results: UCF occurred in 8.9% (7/79) of caudal block and 7.3% (6/82) of penile block patients (RR=0.98; 95% CI 0.35–2.76; p=0.9); caudal block group received less intraoperative (33% vs 56%, p<0.001) and rescue opioids (4.9% vs 15.7%, p=0.01), and had lower mean PACU FLACC pain scores (0.49±1.34 vs 1.14±2.3, p=0.03).
- Limitations:
- Incomplete enrollment
- Loss to follow-up
- Wide confidence intervals limit precision
- Early trial termination
- Clinically important differences cannot be excluded
- Why this matters: This study provides prospective evidence to inform anesthetic choice in pediatric hypospadias repair, suggesting caudal block may reduce opioid use and pain without increasing fistula risk.

BOTTOM LINE: Maternal nutritional supplementation during lactation increases B-vitamin content in human milk, with limited effects on other milk components, and may improve infant growth in undernourished populations.

- Study type: Harmonized analysis of three randomized controlled trials
- Population/setting: Lactating mothers and their infants in Burkina Faso (MISAME-III), Pakistan (Mumta-LW), and Tanzania (ELICIT)
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Maternal balanced energy-protein (BEP) supplements or nicotinamide versus standard care/placebo
- Primary endpoints: Changes in human milk composition (B-vitamins, macronutrients, oligosaccharides, bioactive proteins, microbiome), and infant growth
- Key results: BEP or nicotinamide supplementation increased milk B-vitamin levels; other milk components were largely unchanged; postnatal BEP improved infant growth only in the more undernourished cohort; maternal and infant blood showed concordant changes in a subset.
- Limitations:
- Limited to three low-resource settings
- Infant growth benefit observed only in the most undernourished cohort
- Not all milk components were affected by supplementation
- Why this matters: Extending maternal supplementation into lactation can improve milk micronutrient quality and may benefit infant growth in populations at risk of undernutrition.

pubmed.bottom_line: This Bayesian meta-analysis of eight studies (6,847 patients) found that mechanical ventilation during CPR in adult cardiac arrest was associated with higher rates of return of spontaneous circulation compared to manual bag-valve ventilation, but evidence for improved survival and neurological outcomes remains inconclusive; this suggests MV may improve immediate resuscitation success, though its impact on longer-term outcomes is uncertain.

cybermed_stored_deep_dive.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: Mechanical ventilation during CPR in adult cardiac arrest is associated with higher rates of return of spontaneous circulation compared to manual bag-valve ventilation, but evidence for improved survival and neurological outcomes is inconclusive.

- Study type: Systematic review and Bayesian meta-analysis
- Population/setting: Adults with cardiac arrest from eight studies involving 6,847 patients
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Mechanical ventilation during CPR versus manual bag-valve ventilation
- Primary endpoints: Return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), survival to hospital admission, survival to hospital discharge, and good neurological outcome
- Key results: Mechanical ventilation was associated with higher ROSC (pooled RR 1.20; 95% CrI 1.04 to 1.42; 99% posterior probability of benefit); posterior probabilities favoring MV for survival to admission, discharge, and favorable neurological outcome were 92.3%, 93.6%, and 92.2%, respectively; pneumothorax incidence was similar between groups.
- Limitations:
- Evidence for survival and neurological outcomes is imprecise and inconclusive
- Limited number of included studies
- Potential heterogeneity in study designs and patient populations
- Why this matters: This analysis informs resuscitation practices by suggesting mechanical ventilation may improve ROSC during CPR, though benefits for longer-term outcomes remain uncertain.

pubmed.bottom_line: In this single-center randomized controlled trial of 143 patients undergoing elective noncardiac surgery, a mean arterial pressure alarm set at 72 mmHg was found to be noninferior to the Hypotension Prediction Index alarm for preventing intraoperative hypotension, suggesting that simpler MAP alarms may be as effective as more complex predictive algorithms for blood pressure management during surgery.

cybermed_stored_deep_dive.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: A mean arterial pressure alarm set at 72 mmHg is noninferior to the Hypotension Prediction Index (HPI) alarm (>85) for preventing intraoperative hypotension in moderate- or high-risk elective noncardiac surgery, offering a simple and cost-effective alternative.

- Study type: Single-center, blinded, randomized controlled noninferiority trial
- Population/setting: Adults (n=143) undergoing moderate- or high-risk elective noncardiac surgery with continuous arterial pressure monitoring at a tertiary referral center in the Netherlands.
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Mean arterial pressure alarm (<72 mmHg) versus Hypotension Prediction Index alarm (>85).
- Primary endpoints: Area under the threshold for mean arterial pressure <65 mmHg (cumulative exposure to hypotension).
- Key results: Median area under the hypotension threshold was 3.75 [0.00–22.62] mmHg·min (MAP group) vs 4.00 [0.00–19.00] mmHg·min (HPI group); mean difference after log-transformation was 0.03 (95% CI, -0.24 to 0.29), above the noninferiority margin. No significant differences were found in secondary hemodynamic metrics, alarm characteristics, patient outcomes, or administered medications and fluids.
- Limitations:
- Single-center design limits generalizability.
- Blinding was achieved with a custom monitor cover, but complete blinding of clinical staff may not be feasible.
- Some missing laboratory data for secondary outcomes (e.g., AKI, myocardial injury).
- No predefined treatment protocol for alarm response.
- Why this matters: Using a widely available and simple mean arterial pressure alarm at 72 mmHg is as effective as the proprietary HPI algorithm for proactive intraoperative blood pressure management, potentially reducing costs and increasing accessibility.

pubmed.title: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Clinical Decision Support for Postoperative Delirium Prevention: A Pragmatic Randomized Controlled Trial.
pubmed.bottom_line: A statistically significant benefit was not demonstrated; this does not prove absence of an effect. Interpret secondary signals cautiously. Reported results: Delirium assessments were documented in 1255 patients. In those assessed, delirium occurred in 225/641 (35.1%) in the intervention group versus 201/614 (32.7%) in the control group, P=.37; a statistically significant difference was not demonstrated. Limitations: Missing delirium assessments in most randomized patients limit interpretation; absence of statistical significance is not proof of no effect.

pubmed.title: Incidence of general anaesthesia according to urgency of surgery: a multicentre prospective cohort study of 9989 Caesarean deliveries in Europe.
pubmed.bottom_line: In this large, multicentre European cohort study of nearly 10,000 Caesarean deliveries, general anaesthesia was used five times more often in emergency cases (54%) than in elective cases (10.9%), highlighting the continued reliance on GA in urgent situations; these robust, contemporary data can inform anaesthetic planning and resource allocation for Caesarean deliveries.

pubmed_facts.design: Journal Article
pubmed_facts.population: Pragmatic, effectiveness, open-label, superiority, randomized clinical trial in 14 intensive care units (ICUs) in Canada. Adults (≥18 years) receiving sedation for less than 72 hours and receiving mechanical ventilation for AHRF from non-COVID respiratory failure (ratio of partial pressure of arterial oxygen [Pao2] to fraction of inspired oxygen [Fio2] <300 mm Hg) or COVID-19 were enrolled between September 2020 and March 2025 with follow-up through June 2025.
pubmed_facts.intervention_comparator: Patients were randomized to an inhaled sedation strategy using isoflurane with intravenous adjuncts as clinically needed or to a usual intravenous sedation care strategy. Sedatives were titrated to achieve the desired target sedation score guided by clinical teams and continued until extubation or death.
pubmed_facts.primary_endpoint: Primary outcome was all-cause hospital mortality. Secondary outcomes included ICU- and ventilator-free days at day 30; hospital-free days at day 60; use of refractory hypoxemia adjunctive therapies; delirium- and coma-free days at day 14; and quality-of-life and disability scores at 3 months.
pubmed_facts.reported_results:
Of 786 patients randomized, 780 were included in the primary analysis (mean age, 61.1 years; 34.0% female; 73.7% non-COVID AHRF, mean Pao2:Fio2 ratio, 152.6 mm Hg); 385 in the inhaled sedation and 395 in the intravenous sedation groups. In the inhaled sedation group, 49.9% to 55.4% of patients received concomitant intravenous sedation on any day during the first 14 days after randomization. At hospital discharge, 161 of 379 patients (42.5%) in the inhaled sedation group had died, compared with 171 of 390 patients (43.8%) in the intravenous sedation group (risk ratio, 0.98 [95% CI, 0.84 to 1.14]; P = .85). There was no effect modification in prespecified subgroup analyses for age, sex, and COVID-19 status. ICU-, ventilator-, and hospital-free days were similar between groups. The inhaled sedation group received more adjunctive therapies for hypoxemia (239 [63.9%] vs 214 [55.0%]; between-group difference, 8.89% [95% CI, 1.95% to 15.83%]) and had fewer delirium- and coma-free days (between-group difference, -0.95 [95% CI, -1.69 to -0.22]). There was no difference in quality-of-life and disability scores between groups.
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In mechanically ventilated adults with AHRF, an inhaled sedation strategy using isoflurane with intravenous adjuncts as clinically needed did not reduce hospital mortality compared with an intravenous sedation strategy.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04415060.

pubmed_shared_synopsis.population_setting: Pragmatic, effectiveness, open-label, superiority, randomized clinical trial in 14 intensive care units (ICUs) in Canada. Adults (≥18 years) receiving sedation for less than 72 hours and receiving mechanical ventilation for AHRF from non-COVID respiratory failure (ratio of partial pressure of arterial oxygen [Pao2] to fraction of inspired oxygen [Fio2] <300 mm Hg) or COVID-19 were enrolled between September 2020 and March 2025 with follow-up through June 2025.
pubmed_shared_synopsis.intervention_or_exposure: Patients were randomized to an inhaled sedation strategy using isoflurane with intravenous adjuncts as clinically needed or to a usual intravenous sedation care strategy. Sedatives were titrated to achieve the desired target sedation score guided by clinical teams and continued until extubation or death.
pubmed_shared_synopsis.primary_endpoint: Primary outcome was all-cause hospital mortality. Secondary outcomes included ICU- and ventilator-free days at day 30; hospital-free days at day 60; use of refractory hypoxemia adjunctive therapies; delirium- and coma-free days at day 14; and quality-of-life and disability scores at 3 months.
pubmed_shared_synopsis.key_results: The inhaled sedation group received more adjunctive therapies for hypoxemia (239 [63.9%] vs 214 [55.0%]; between-group difference, 8.89% [95% CI, 1.95% to 15.83%]) and had fewer delirium- and coma-free days (between-group difference, -0.95 [95% CI, -1.69 to -0.22]). CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In mechanically ventilated adults with AHRF, an inhaled sedation strategy using isoflurane with intravenous adjuncts as clinically needed did not reduce hospital mortality compared with an intravenous sedation strategy.
pubmed_shared_synopsis.key_secondary_results: Of 786 patients randomized, 780 were included in the primary analysis (mean age, 61.1 years; 34.0% female; 73.7% non-COVID AHRF, mean Pao2:Fio2 ratio, 152.6 mm Hg); 385 in the inhaled sedation and 395 in the intravenous sedation groups. In the inhaled sedation group, 49.9% to 55.4% of patients received concomitant intravenous sedation on any day during the first 14 days after randomization. At hospital discharge, 161 of 379 patients (42.5%) in the inhaled sedation group had died, compared with 171 of 390 patients (43.8%) in the intravenous sedation group (risk ratio, 0.98 [95% CI, 0.84 to 1.14]; P = .85). There was no difference in quality-of-life and disability scores between groups. TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04415060.

pubmed_facts.design: Journal Article
pubmed_facts.population: Cluster-randomized, cluster-crossover, pragmatic clinical strategy trial including adult patients receiving vasopressors for septic shock at 13 hospitals in Idaho and Utah from February 1, 2024, to July 31, 2025. The last day of follow-up for the primary outcome was February 17, 2026.
pubmed_facts.intervention_comparator: Hospital-level implementation of septic shock management strategies recommending fixed-dose vasopressin initiation when the total dose of other vasopressors reached 0.1 µg/kg/min of norepinephrine or equivalent (lower-threshold strategy) or when the total dose of other vasopressors reached 0.4 µg/kg/min of norepinephrine or equivalent (higher-threshold strategy). Hospitals were randomized for the first month to an initial strategy (6 hospitals to the lower threshold vs 7 hospitals to the higher threshold) and then crossed over to the alternate strategy monthly thereafter.
pubmed_facts.primary_endpoint: The primary outcome of 28-day mortality and the key secondary outcome of kidney replacement therapy-free days through day 28 were analyzed using multivariable generalized linear mixed-effects models, accounting for trial site and baseline patient characteristics.
pubmed_facts.reported_results:
There were 3959 unique patients with septic shock (median age, 68 [IQR, 57 to 77] years; 1903 [48%] were female). Of the patients more likely to experience differential management under the tested hospital-level vasopressin dose strategies (maximum vasopressor dose ≥0.07 µg/kg/min of norepinephrine or equivalent), 1034 of 1521 (68.0%) cared for under the lower-threshold strategy received vasopressin compared with 651 of 1526 (42.7%) cared for under the higher-threshold strategy. In the hospital-level strategy recommending a lower-dose threshold for vasopressin initiation, the maximum vasopressor dose received prior to vasopressin initiation was a median of 0.14 (IQR, 0.10 to 0.22) µg/kg/min of norepinephrine or equivalent vs 0.34 (IQR, 0.16 to 0.42) µg/kg/min of norepinephrine or equivalent in the hospital-level strategy recommending a higher-dose threshold for vasopressin initiation. Mortality at 28 days occurred in 628 of 1975 patients (31.8%) treated with the hospital-level strategy recommending initiation of vasopressin at a lower-dose threshold of other vasopressors vs 655 of 1984 patients (33.0%) treated with the higher-threshold strategy (adjusted marginal odds ratio, 0.98 [95% CI, 0.87 to 1.06], P = .62; adjusted risk difference, -0.4 [95% CI, -2.7 to 1.3] percentage points). Patients in both strategies for vasopressin initiation had a median of 29 (IQR, -1 to 29) kidney replacement therapy-free days (adjusted marginal odds ratio, 1.01 [95% CI, 0.91 to 1.14]).
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In this large, pragmatic clinical trial comparing the effectiveness of 2 hospital-level strategies for second-line vasopressor management in septic shock, a strategy recommending initiation of vasopressin at a lower dose of other vasopressors did not reduce 28-day mortality compared with a strategy recommending vasopressin initiation at a higher dose of other vasopressors.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT06217562.

pubmed.title: The role of fibrinogen concentrate in the reduction of allogeneic blood product requirements: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
pubmed.bottom_line: This large meta-analysis (58 studies, 13,530 patients) shows that fibrinogen concentrate significantly reduces the need for allogeneic blood product transfusions in adults with acquired hypofibrinogenaemia, without increasing mortality or thromboembolic risk, supporting its use as a safe and effective alternative to other treatments, particularly in cardiac surgery.

pubmed_facts.reported_results:
Eighty-eight patients were enrolled (44 HFCWO, 44 control), with comparable baseline characteristics. Bronchoscopy was required in 6 patients (13.6%) versus 14 (31.8%) (unadjusted p=0.042); after adjustment the association did not retain statistical significance (adjusted OR 0.336, 95% CI 0.111-1.021; p=0.055). Secondary outcomes, analyzed without correction for multiple testing, are exploratory. Hospital stay (12 [10-15.5] vs 16.5 [13-21] days) and RICU stay (8 [7-10.5] vs 12 [9-17] days) were shorter, with adjusted reductions of 4.5 and 3.6 days. HFNC duration was shorter (6 [4-8] vs 9.5 [6-11.5] days) and remained significant after adjustment, whereas the reduction in NIV duration did not (adjusted p=0.166). No patient required intubation and mortality did not differ.
INTERPRETATION: In this exploratory trial, HFCWO did not significantly reduce the need for therapeutic bronchoscopy after adjustment. Associated reductions in LOS and HFNC duration are hypothesis-generating and require confirmation in adequately powered multicenter trials.

Abstract / methods: We conducted a retrospective target-trial emulation of 2016-2025 high-resolution electronic health records from Zigong Fourth People's Hospital. Adults with sepsis, final or corrected iCa of 0.90-1.10 mmol/L, and no emergency indication were eligible at result availability. Strategies were executed calcium within 2 h versus no calcium through 6 h; care after 6 h was unrestricted. Clone-censor weighting and overlap tilting addressed grace periods, measured time-varying confounding, and clinical equipoise. The primary outcome was being alive and vasopressor-free at 24 h. Estimates and two-sided 95% percentile intervals came from 2,000 patient-level bootstrap samples with model refitting.
Abstract / background: Intravenous calcium is frequently administered during sepsis, yet whether early treatment improves 24-h hemodynamic recovery remains uncertain. We compared 24-h hemodynamic recovery between calcium initiation within 2 h of a non-emergency low-ionized calcium (iCa) result and no calcium initiation during the first 6 h after the result.

pubmed.population_setting: This prospective, randomized, single-center pilot study involved 76 S-PAKI patients who required CRRT. Participants were randomly assigned to receive either CVVH combined with hemoadsorption (CVVH + HA group, n = 38) or conventional CVVH therapy (CVVH group, n = 38). A post hoc exploratory subgroup analysis revealed that among patients with Chemokine (C-C motif) ligand 14 (CCL14) levels greater than 1.3 ng/ml, the mortality risk in the CVVH + HA group was lower than that in the CVVH group.

clinical_context.uncertainty: No statistically significant benefit demonstrated; no-effect/equivalence not established

clinical_summary.text: In this pilot randomized trial of 76 patients with sepsis-associated persistent severe AKI requiring CRRT, adding hemoadsorption to CVVH did not significantly reduce 30-day all-cause mortality compared to CVVH alone. Secondary outcomes showed improvements in organ dysfunction scores and cytokine clearance, but no significant benefit in renal recovery or length of ICU/hospital stay. A post hoc subgroup suggested possible mortality benefit in patients with high urinary CCL14, but this requires confirmation.
clinical_summary.result_quote: The CVVH + HA group showed a statistically non-significant trend to lower 30-day all-cause mortality compared to the CVVH group (36.8% vs. 52.6%, P = 0.159).

pubmed_facts.primary_endpoint: The primary endpoint was 30-day all-cause mortality.
pubmed_facts.reported_results: The CVVH + HA group showed a statistically non-significant trend to lower 30-day all-cause mortality compared to the CVVH group (36.8% vs. 52.6%, P = 0.159). A post hoc exploratory subgroup analysis revealed that among patients with Chemokine (C-C motif) ligand 14 (CCL14) levels greater than 1.3 ng/ml, the mortality risk in the CVVH + HA group was lower than that in the CVVH group. In terms of secondary outcomes, hemoadsorption therapy significantly decreased APACHE II and SOFA scores, enhanced cytokine clearance, and improved hemodynamic status; however, it did not lead to significant improvements in renal functional prognosis, nor did it shorten the duration of mechanical ventilation, renal replacement therapy, ICU stay, or overall hospital stay among survivors.

Abstract / methods: We conducted a nationwide cross-sectional survey among French anesthesiologists and nurse anesthetists in November 2025 to assess ventilatory settings during abdominal surgery, both for laparotomy and laparoscopy. Protective ventilation was defined as the combination of low tidal volume (6-8 mL/kg predicted body weight), low-to-moderate PEEP (5-8 cm H2O), and recruitment maneuvers. Individualization of PEEP was defined as the use of driving pressure, mechanical power, or compliance to titrate PEEP.
Abstract / background: Data are lacking regarding current ventilatory settings during abdominal surgery. Expert recommendations emphasize the need for protective ventilation, and several tools are now available to individualize positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP).

clinical_summary.text: This systematic review examined how often sex, race, and ethnicity were reported in US-based randomized controlled trials of regional anesthesia for total joint arthroplasty, comparing published articles and ClinicalTrials.gov entries. While sex was reported in nearly all studies, race and ethnicity were infrequently captured in both sources, with no significant association between reporting and study characteristics. These findings highlight a lack of standardized demographic reporting, which may limit the generalizability and equity of research in this field.

pubmed_facts.evidence: Abstract / unstructured: Regional anesthesia provides significant perioperative benefits, including improved pain control and reduced opioid consumption. Clinical trial evidence underpins anesthetic practice, yet inadequate demographic representation and reporting may limit the ability to likely evaluate findings and perpetuate inequities. This systematic review assessed the reporting of race, ethnicity, and sex in randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of regional anesthesia for total joint arthroplasty (TJA). The Aggregate Analysis of Clinical Trials (AACT) database was searched for US-based interventional RCTs of regional anesthesia for TJA published from 2015 to 2025. Trials were required to be registered and published in English. Exclusion criteria included conference abstracts, duplicate publications, and non-peer-reviewed reports. Data on trial characteristics, sample size, interventions, and participant demographics were compared from published articles and ClinicalTrials.gov. The primary outcome was reporting of participant sex, race, and ethnicity in publications and registry entries. Secondary outcomes included demographic distributions across racial and ethnic groups and associations between reporting and study characteristics (funding source, year of publication, center type, US region, sample size) using Fisher's exact test. Twenty-nine RCTs were included in the final analysis, representing 2914 participants. Of 29 journal articles, 28 studies (96.6%) reported sex, 14 (48.3%) reported race, and five (17.2%) reported ethnicity in the published journal articles. Among studies reporting race, 1068 (78.5%) participants identified as White, 253 (18.6%) as Black, 30 (2.2%) as other, 6 (0.4%) as Asian or Pacific Islander, and one (0.07%) as Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander. Conversely, the data from ClinicalTrials.gov reveals that of the same 29 studies, 22 (75.9%) reported sex, 12 (41.4%) reported race, and seven (24.1%) reported ethnicity. Trial characteristics did not show statistically significant associations when comparing studies that did versus did not report race, ethnicity, or sex. In this review of demographic reporting of US-based regional anesthesia RCTs for TJA, sex was consistently reported, whereas race and ethnicity were infrequently captured. The lack of difference in reporting practices across various trial characteristics points toward a broader issue within the field of regional anesthesia for TJA. Notable inconsistencies in demographic reporting on ClinicalTrials.gov were also observed. The absence of standardized demographic reporting underscores the need for journals to mandate consistent reporting practices in clinical research. Efforts to recruit more diverse study populations are essential to enhance the applicability of trial results and to address ongoing inequities in access to care and patient outcomes following TJA.

pubmed_facts.reported_results:
Among 584 patients (median [IQR] age, 67.5 [55.0-76.0] years; 192 [32.9%] females), new-onset or worsening AKI within 7 postoperative days occurred in 22.8% (66/290) randomized to receive dobutamine plus norepinephrine vs 34.7% (102/294) randomized to receive norepinephrine alone (adjusted risk ratio [ARR], 0.64 [95% CI, 0.49-0.83]). No significant differences were observed in 9 of the 11 secondary outcomes. SOFA scores on postoperative day 1 (adjusted difference, -0.53 [95% CI, -0.98 to -0.07]) were lower and urine output 1 hour post intervention (adjusted difference, 0.55 [95% CI, 0.03 to 1.07] mL/kg/h) was higher in the dobutamine plus norepinephrine group. Stage 2 and 3 AKI were lower in the dobutamine plus norepinephrine group compared with the norepinephrine alone group (stage 2: 4.8% vs 9.9%; ARR, 0.48 [95% CI, 0.26-0.88]; stage 3: 7.9% vs 13.6%; ARR, 0.56 [95% CI, 0.35-0.91]). Tachycardia (heart rate >100/min) occurred more frequently in patients receiving dobutamine and norepinephrine than norepinephrine alone.
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: Among adult patients with septic shock undergoing surgical source control, intraoperative dobutamine combined with norepinephrine reduced the incidence of new-onset or worsening AKI within 7 postoperative days compared with norepinephrine.

Abstract / methods: In a randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial at a single US government hospital, veterans aged 20 to 60 with fibromyalgia were assigned to active or sham in-home CES, stratified by sex. Abstract / background: Fibromyalgia is a chronic pain disorder frequently co-occurring with depression, anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and insomnia, particularly in veterans, and safer nonpharmacological therapies are needed. Cranial electrotherapy stimulation, also referred to as cranial electrotherapy stimulation (CES), may help with anxiety and sleep, but its effect on pain is unclear. This feasibility study evaluated magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to identify neural correlates of pain and treatment response for CES effects on fibromyalgia pain in veterans.

deep_dives.title: Mechanical versus manual bag-valve ventilation during cardiopulmonary resuscitation in adults with cardiac arrest: A systematic review and Bayesian meta-analysis.
deep_dives.bottom_line: This Bayesian meta-analysis of eight studies (6,847 patients) found that mechanical ventilation during CPR in adult cardiac arrest was associated with higher rates of return of spontaneous circulation compared to manual bag-valve ventilation, but evidence for improved survival and neurological outcomes remains inconclusive; this suggests MV may improve immediate resuscitation success, though its impact on longer-term outcomes is uncertain.
deep_dives.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: Mechanical ventilation during CPR in adult cardiac arrest is associated with higher rates of return of spontaneous circulation compared to manual bag-valve ventilation, but evidence for improved survival and neurological outcomes is inconclusive.

- Study type: Systematic review and Bayesian meta-analysis
- Population/setting: Adults with cardiac arrest from eight studies involving 6,847 patients
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Mechanical ventilation during CPR versus manual bag-valve ventilation
- Primary endpoints: Return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), survival to hospital admission, survival to hospital discharge, and good neurological outcome
- Key results: Mechanical ventilation was associated with higher ROSC (pooled RR 1.20; 95% CrI 1.04 to 1.42; 99% posterior probability of benefit); posterior probabilities favoring MV for survival to admission, discharge, and favorable neurological outcome were 92.3%, 93.6%, and 92.2%, respectively; pneumothorax incidence was similar between groups.
- Limitations:
- Evidence for survival and neurological outcomes is imprecise and inconclusive
- Limited number of included studies
- Potential heterogeneity in study designs and patient populations
- Why this matters: This analysis informs resuscitation practices by suggesting mechanical ventilation may improve ROSC during CPR, though benefits for longer-term outcomes remain uncertain.

deep_dives.title: Hypotension Prediction Index versus Mean Arterial Pressure Alarm for Preventing Intraoperative Hypotension in Elective Noncardiac Surgery: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
deep_dives.bottom_line: In this single-center randomized controlled trial of 143 patients undergoing elective noncardiac surgery, a mean arterial pressure alarm set at 72 mmHg was found to be noninferior to the Hypotension Prediction Index alarm for preventing intraoperative hypotension, suggesting that simpler MAP alarms may be as effective as more complex predictive algorithms for blood pressure management during surgery.
deep_dives.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: A mean arterial pressure alarm set at 72 mmHg is noninferior to the Hypotension Prediction Index (HPI) alarm (>85) for preventing intraoperative hypotension in moderate- or high-risk elective noncardiac surgery, offering a simple and cost-effective alternative.

- Study type: Single-center, blinded, randomized controlled noninferiority trial
- Population/setting: Adults (n=143) undergoing moderate- or high-risk elective noncardiac surgery with continuous arterial pressure monitoring at a tertiary referral center in the Netherlands.
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Mean arterial pressure alarm (<72 mmHg) versus Hypotension Prediction Index alarm (>85).
- Primary endpoints: Area under the threshold for mean arterial pressure <65 mmHg (cumulative exposure to hypotension).
- Key results: Median area under the hypotension threshold was 3.75 [0.00–22.62] mmHg·min (MAP group) vs 4.00 [0.00–19.00] mmHg·min (HPI group); mean difference after log-transformation was 0.03 (95% CI, -0.24 to 0.29), above the noninferiority margin. No significant differences were found in secondary hemodynamic metrics, alarm characteristics, patient outcomes, or administered medications and fluids.
- Limitations:
- Single-center design limits generalizability.
- Blinding was achieved with a custom monitor cover, but complete blinding of clinical staff may not be feasible.
- Some missing laboratory data for secondary outcomes (e.g., AKI, myocardial injury).
- No predefined treatment protocol for alarm response.
- Why this matters: Using a widely available and simple mean arterial pressure alarm at 72 mmHg is as effective as the proprietary HPI algorithm for proactive intraoperative blood pressure management, potentially reducing costs and increasing accessibility.

pubmed_facts.population: Pragmatic, effectiveness, open-label, superiority, randomized clinical trial in 14 intensive care units (ICUs) in Canada. Adults (≥18 years) receiving sedation for less than 72 hours and receiving mechanical ventilation for AHRF from non-COVID respiratory failure (ratio of partial pressure of arterial oxygen [Pao2] to fraction of inspired oxygen [Fio2] <300 mm Hg) or COVID-19 were enrolled between September 2020 and March 2025 with follow-up through June 2025.
pubmed_facts.intervention_comparator: Patients were randomized to an inhaled sedation strategy using isoflurane with intravenous adjuncts as clinically needed or to a usual intravenous sedation care strategy. Sedatives were titrated to achieve the desired target sedation score guided by clinical teams and continued until extubation or death.
pubmed_facts.primary_endpoint: Primary outcome was all-cause hospital mortality. Secondary outcomes included ICU- and ventilator-free days at day 30; hospital-free days at day 60; use of refractory hypoxemia adjunctive therapies; delirium- and coma-free days at day 14; and quality-of-life and disability scores at 3 months.
pubmed_facts.reported_results:
Of 786 patients randomized, 780 were included in the primary analysis (mean age, 61.1 years; 34.0% female; 73.7% non-COVID AHRF, mean Pao2:Fio2 ratio, 152.6 mm Hg); 385 in the inhaled sedation and 395 in the intravenous sedation groups. In the inhaled sedation group, 49.9% to 55.4% of patients received concomitant intravenous sedation on any day during the first 14 days after randomization. At hospital discharge, 161 of 379 patients (42.5%) in the inhaled sedation group had died, compared with 171 of 390 patients (43.8%) in the intravenous sedation group (risk ratio, 0.98 [95% CI, 0.84 to 1.14]; P = .85). There was no effect modification in prespecified subgroup analyses for age, sex, and COVID-19 status. ICU-, ventilator-, and hospital-free days were similar between groups. The inhaled sedation group received more adjunctive therapies for hypoxemia (239 [63.9%] vs 214 [55.0%]; between-group difference, 8.89% [95% CI, 1.95% to 15.83%]) and had fewer delirium- and coma-free days (between-group difference, -0.95 [95% CI, -1.69 to -0.22]). There was no difference in quality-of-life and disability scores between groups.
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In mechanically ventilated adults with AHRF, an inhaled sedation strategy using isoflurane with intravenous adjuncts as clinically needed did not reduce hospital mortality compared with an intravenous sedation strategy.

pubmed_facts.design: Journal Article
pubmed_facts.population: Cluster-randomized, cluster-crossover, pragmatic clinical strategy trial including adult patients receiving vasopressors for septic shock at 13 hospitals in Idaho and Utah from February 1, 2024, to July 31, 2025. The last day of follow-up for the primary outcome was February 17, 2026.
pubmed_facts.intervention_comparator: Hospital-level implementation of septic shock management strategies recommending fixed-dose vasopressin initiation when the total dose of other vasopressors reached 0.1 µg/kg/min of norepinephrine or equivalent (lower-threshold strategy) or when the total dose of other vasopressors reached 0.4 µg/kg/min of norepinephrine or equivalent (higher-threshold strategy). Hospitals were randomized for the first month to an initial strategy (6 hospitals to the lower threshold vs 7 hospitals to the higher threshold) and then crossed over to the alternate strategy monthly thereafter.
pubmed_facts.primary_endpoint: The primary outcome of 28-day mortality and the key secondary outcome of kidney replacement therapy-free days through day 28 were analyzed using multivariable generalized linear mixed-effects models, accounting for trial site and baseline patient characteristics.
pubmed_facts.reported_results:
There were 3959 unique patients with septic shock (median age, 68 [IQR, 57 to 77] years; 1903 [48%] were female). Of the patients more likely to experience differential management under the tested hospital-level vasopressin dose strategies (maximum vasopressor dose ≥0.07 µg/kg/min of norepinephrine or equivalent), 1034 of 1521 (68.0%) cared for under the lower-threshold strategy received vasopressin compared with 651 of 1526 (42.7%) cared for under the higher-threshold strategy. In the hospital-level strategy recommending a lower-dose threshold for vasopressin initiation, the maximum vasopressor dose received prior to vasopressin initiation was a median of 0.14 (IQR, 0.10 to 0.22) µg/kg/min of norepinephrine or equivalent vs 0.34 (IQR, 0.16 to 0.42) µg/kg/min of norepinephrine or equivalent in the hospital-level strategy recommending a higher-dose threshold for vasopressin initiation. Mortality at 28 days occurred in 628 of 1975 patients (31.8%) treated with the hospital-level strategy recommending initiation of vasopressin at a lower-dose threshold of other vasopressors vs 655 of 1984 patients (33.0%) treated with the higher-threshold strategy (adjusted marginal odds ratio, 0.98 [95% CI, 0.87 to 1.06], P = .62; adjusted risk difference, -0.4 [95% CI, -2.7 to 1.3] percentage points). Patients in both strategies for vasopressin initiation had a median of 29 (IQR, -1 to 29) kidney replacement therapy-free days (adjusted marginal odds ratio, 1.01 [95% CI, 0.91 to 1.14]).
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In this large, pragmatic clinical trial comparing the effectiveness of 2 hospital-level strategies for second-line vasopressor management in septic shock, a strategy recommending initiation of vasopressin at a lower dose of other vasopressors did not reduce 28-day mortality compared with a strategy recommending vasopressin initiation at a higher dose of other vasopressors.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT06217562.

pubmed_facts.design: We conducted a retrospective target-trial emulation of 2016-2025 high-resolution electronic health records from Zigong Fourth People's Hospital.
pubmed_facts.population: Of 5,993 patients, 1,538 initiated calcium within 2 h, 147 initiated at 2-6 h, and 4,308 received none through 6 h; none of the latter initiated calcium during 6-24 h.
pubmed_facts.intervention_comparator: Strategies were executed calcium within 2 h versus no calcium through 6 h; care after 6 h was unrestricted.
pubmed_facts.primary_endpoint: The primary outcome was being alive and vasopressor-free at 24 h.
pubmed_facts.reported_results: Of 5,993 patients, 1,538 initiated calcium within 2 h, 147 initiated at 2-6 h, and 4,308 received none through 6 h; none of the latter initiated calcium during 6-24 h. The standardized probability of 24-h hemodynamic recovery was 69.9% with early calcium and 61.1% with deferral, corresponding to a risk difference of + 8.69 percentage points (95% percentile interval, + 4.66 to + 12.84) and a risk ratio of 1.142 (1.074-1.214). The estimated association varied with baseline norepinephrine-equivalent dose (Holm-adjusted P = 2.00 × 10⁻⁶), whereas the iCa interaction did not remain statistically supported after adjustment (P = 0.097). pubmed_facts.reported_results: Among 234 included events, 86 events (36.8%) had guideline-recommended (20-30 beats per min [bpm]) average ventilation rates during CPR. The association between guideline-recommended CPR ventilation rate and survival to hospital discharge was evaluated with Poisson regression using generalized estimating equations, controlling for a priori covariables (initial pulse status, immediate cause of arrest). We found no association between guideline-recommended ventilation rates and survival to hospital discharge (adjusted relative risk [aRR], 0.95; 95% CI, 0.75-1.21; p = 0.68). In exploratory analyses, novel age-stratified ventilation rates were identified using natural cubic splines and subsequently evaluated in multivariable models. We identified potential thresholds (< 8 yr, ≥ 26 bpm; ≥ 8 yr, < 26 bpm). For children younger than 8 years, average CPR ventilation rate greater than or equal to 26 bpm was associated with improved survival to hospital discharge compared with less than 26 bpm (aRR, 1.32; 95% CI, 1.00-1.73; p = 0.048).

Abstract / conclusions: Open/flexible ICU family presence may reduce delirium and shorten the duration of IMV slightly, without increasing infections or ICU mortality, although the certainty of evidence is low and heterogeneity remains substantial.
Abstract / objectives: To critically evaluate the comparative effects of open or flexible family presence policies vs. restricted or traditional family presence policies on the occurrence of delirium and other major outcomes among adult patients admitted to ICUs. DATA SOURCES: We conducted a comprehensive electronic search of MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, CINAHL, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials from inception to November 21, 2025. STUDY SELECTION: We included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing open or flexible vs. restricted ICU visiting policies in adult patients. DATA EXTRACTION: The primary outcome extracted was delirium occurrence. Secondary outcomes included the duration of invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV), ICU length of stay, hospital-acquired infections, and ICU mortality. DATA SYNTHESIS: Thirteen RCTs comprising 3861 patients were included. Random-effects models showed that compared with restricted policies, open/flexible family presence reduced delirium occurrence (risk ratio [RR], 0.48; 95% CI, 0.29-0.81; low certainty) and IMV duration (mean difference [MD], -0.36 d; 95% CI, -0.46 to -0.26 d; low certainty).

pubmed_facts.primary_endpoint: The primary outcome was POD incidence (risk ratio [RR]).
pubmed_facts.reported_results: Twenty-five RCTs (3344 patients) were included (ketamine: 9; esketamine: 16). Both agents reduced POD risk versus control (ketamine: RR 0.69, 95% CI, 0.49-0.98, P = .04; esketamine: RR 0.58, 95% CI, 0.36-0.95, P = .03). Benefit was more evident with high-dose regimens (single bolus: ketamine >0.5 mg/kg or esketamine >0.25 mg/kg; cumulative dose: ketamine >1.0 mg/kg or esketamine >0.5 mg/kg), bolus-plus-infusion, and in major surgery. The effect was observed when POD was assessed 2 to 7 days postoperatively, but not within 24 hours. TSA indicated that current evidence remains inconclusive due to insufficient information size. Dizziness risk increased (RR 1.45, 95% CI, 1.14-1.84, P = .002), while postoperative depressive symptoms decreased (RR 0.78, 95% CI, 0.63-0.96, P = .02; based on 2 studies, 493 patients).
pubmed_facts.conclusions: Perioperative ketamine and esketamine show a potential signal for POD reduction, particularly with optimized dosing in high‑risk patients. However, the evidence is currently inconclusive, and increased dizziness risk precludes routine recommendation. Large, multicenter RCTs are urgently needed.

clinical_summary.text: In this scoping review of nine observational studies on patients undergoing ECMO weaning, various blood processing strategies—including autologous blood reinfusion and direct discard—were compared. The authors found that autologous blood reinfusion appears feasible and is associated with improved surrogate hematological outcomes versus direct discard, but due to limited, low-quality, and heterogeneous evidence, no conclusions can be drawn regarding effects on major clinical outcomes. Further high-quality studies are needed to determine long-term efficacy and safety.
clinical_summary.result_quote: A total of 68 articles were retrieved, and 9 studies were finally included. The identified blood processing strategies were classified into four categories: blood cell salvage system (BCS) autologous reinfusion, pump-controlled blood reinfusion, modified CPD blood bag storage reinfusion, and direct discard.

Abstract / methods: This scoping review strictly followed the PRISMA‑ScR 2018 checklist and JBI methodology. We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science Core Collection, Cochrane Library, CNKI, and Wanfang from inception to March 28, 2026. Two reviewers independently screened literature, extracted data, and assessed quality. Descriptive synthesis and qualitative analysis were performed due to high heterogeneity and lack of randomized controlled trials (RCTs).
Abstract / background: Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) has been widely used for life support in severe refractory cardiac and respiratory failure. During ECMO weaning, the circuit usually retains 500-800 mL of residual blood. Direct discarding leads to blood loss, increased anemia, and higher allogeneic transfusion requirements, while appropriate autologous blood reinfusion can reduce transfusion risks and medical costs. However, evidence on blood processing strategies during ECMO weaning remains scattered, and no unified clinical guidelines exist.

pubmed_facts.reported_results: We included 17 RCTs (N=2288). NIRS-guided management probably reduces early postoperative cognitive decline (risk ratio [RR] 0.65, 95% CI 0.42-0.99; I2=65%, moderate certainty), may have little or no effect on stroke (RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.42-1.91; low certainty) or mortality (RR 0.84, 95% CI 0.47-1.52; low certainty), and may have no effect on delirium (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.56-1.09; I2=32%, low certainty). Findings were primarily derived from small, single-centre trials with heterogenous NIRS thresholds and intervention algorithms. Few studies evaluated outcomes beyond 30 days, and none evaluated validated measures of quality of life or function.

Abstract / methods: We searched CENTRAL, CINAHL, Embase, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, and Web of Science for RCTs comparing NIRS-guided intraoperative management with usual care in adults undergoing on-pump cardiac surgery, assessing the outcomes of postoperative cognitive decline, delirium, stroke, mortality, and functional recovery. We pooled data using random-effects meta-analysis and assessed certainty of evidence using GRADE methodology.
Abstract / background: Adverse neurocognitive and functional outcomes are common after cardiac surgery. Cerebral near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) monitors regional cerebral oxygen saturation, allowing clinicians to detect and reverse cerebral desaturation. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs to evaluate whether intraoperative NIRS monitoring improves neurocognitive outcomes after cardiac surgery.

pubmed_facts.reported_results: Fifty studies met the inclusion criteria in the systematic review, with 28 studies providing 43 unique datasets subclassified by type of surgical procedure for analysis. The pooled random-effects mean intraoperative noise level was 70.7 A-weighted dB [dB(A)] (95% CI 69.0-72.3). Subgroup analysis demonstrated the highest exposures in otolaryngology at 78.8 dB(A) (95% CI 72.8-84.7) and orthopaedics at 73.3 dB(A) (95% CI 68.9-77.8). Meta-regression confirmed surgical specialty as a significant predictor of mean exposure (Q=25.8, degrees of freedom=6, P=0.0002).

Abstract / methods: Five databases were searched from inception to May 2026, in accordance with Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines. Studies were eligible for inclusion if they included surgical specialty and a measure of noise sampled recorded with validated sound metres. Studies were eligible for meta-analysis if they included a mean time-weighted average. Two authors undertook searches and risk-of-bias assessment. Meta-regression estimated pooled means, heterogeneity, and variance.
Abstract / background: Intraoperative noise is an occupational hazard with the potential to compromise anaesthetist performance and patient safety. The WHO recommends hospital sound exposure ≤ 35 dB LAeq (A-weighted equivalent continuous sound level), yet noise levels routinely exceed this level. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to determine intraoperative noise levels worldwide.

clinical_summary.text: In high-risk patients undergoing elective major abdominal surgery, individualized cardiac index-guided hemodynamic therapy targeting each patient's preoperative resting cardiac index did not significantly reduce the incidence of a composite outcome (acute kidney injury, acute myocardial injury, severe infectious complications, nonfatal cardiac arrest, or death within 7 days) compared with routine hemodynamic therapy. There were also no differences in the rates of the individual components of this composite outcome between groups.
clinical_summary.result_quote: Among high-risk patients undergoing elective major abdominal surgery, individualized cardiac index-guided hemodynamic therapy targeting the patient's preoperative resting cardiac index did not reduce the incidence of a composite outcome of acute kidney injury, acute myocardial injury, severe infectious complications, nonfatal cardiac arrest, or death within the first 7 postoperative days compared with routine hemodynamic therapy.

pubmed_facts.design: Journal Article
pubmed_facts.population: This multicenter, single-blind, superiority randomized clinical trial enrolled high-risk patients undergoing elective major abdominal surgery between October 8, 2023, and October 25, 2025, at 12 university medical centers in Austria, the Czech Republic, Denmark, Germany, and Spain. The date of last follow-up was January 15, 2026.
pubmed_facts.intervention_comparator: Patients were randomized to individualized cardiac index-guided hemodynamic therapy targeting the patient's preoperative resting cardiac index vs routine hemodynamic therapy (with blinded cardiac index monitoring).
pubmed_facts.primary_endpoint: The primary outcome was a composite of acute kidney injury, acute myocardial injury, severe infectious complications, nonfatal cardiac arrest, or death within the first 7 postoperative days. Secondary outcomes included the individual components of the primary outcome within the first 7 postoperative days.
pubmed_facts.reported_results:
Of the 1128 patients enrolled, 1111 were randomized and 1095 were included in the primary analysis (median age, 67 years [IQR, 59-74 years]; 49.4% were female). The primary outcome occurred in 243 of 549 patients (44.3%) in the individualized cardiac index-guided hemodynamic therapy group vs 256 of 546 patients (46.9%) in the routine hemodynamic therapy group (relative risk, 0.94 [95.1% CI, 0.83-1.08]; P = .38). There were no between-group differences for the incidence of the individual components of the primary outcome within the first 7 postoperative days.
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: Among high-risk patients undergoing elective major abdominal surgery, individualized cardiac index-guided hemodynamic therapy targeting the patient's preoperative resting cardiac index did not reduce the incidence of a composite outcome of acute kidney injury, acute myocardial injury, severe infectious complications, nonfatal cardiac arrest, or death within the first 7 postoperative days compared with routine hemodynamic therapy.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT05648279.

pubmed.population_setting: Serum samples obtained from ACCESS trial patients at baseline and 72 hours were profiled using the Olink Target 96 Inflammation panel. Patients were grouped by treatment arm and by achievement of the trial's composite primary endpoint. After quality control, 70 proteins from 394 paired samples across 197 patients were analyzed to assess differential expression within and between groups over time, evaluate associations with clinical outcomes, and identify immune endotypes using unsupervised clustering. Among patients achieving the primary endpoint, IL6, CXCL9, CXCL10, and IFN-γ were suppressed only in clarithromycin-treated individuals. The identification of distinct inflammatory endotypes suggests biological heterogeneity in CAP and supports future investigation of endotype-guided approaches to identify patients most likely to benefit from immunomodulatory therapies.

pubmed_facts.primary_endpoint: Patients were grouped by treatment arm and by achievement of the trial's composite primary endpoint.
pubmed_facts.reported_results:
IL6 was selectively downregulated on day 4 in the clarithromycin arm, whereas IFN-γ, CXCL9, CXCL10, and SCF decreased over time across both treatment arms, consistent with resolution of inflammation. Among patients achieving the primary endpoint, IL6, CXCL9, CXCL10, and IFN-γ were suppressed only in clarithromycin-treated individuals. Clustering consistently identified two inflammatory endotypes with comparable SOFA, but distinct RSS scores. The endotype with lower RSS demonstrated higher IFN-γ and globally elevated inflammatory protein expression; in that endotype 90-day mortality was decreased with clarithromycin treatment.
INTERPRETATION: Clarithromycin exerts measurable immunomodulatory effects in CAP, characterized by attenuation of pro-inflammatory cytokines, particularly IL6. The identification of distinct inflammatory endotypes suggests biological heterogeneity in CAP and supports future investigation of endotype-guided approaches to identify patients most likely to benefit from immunomodulatory therapies.
CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04724044, EudraCT 2020-004452-15.

pubmed.population_setting: Operating rooms, our clusters, were each randomized in each 4-week blocks to either active or identical-looking sham supplemental air sterilization. All investigators, clinicians, and patients were fully blinded to treatment. At the third interim analysis, the futility boundary on the composite outcome was crossed for inpatients and for all patients. Enrollment thus stopped with 58,938 randomized inpatients. The primary composite outcome occurred in 8.1% (n=2,389) of inpatients randomized to active purification versus 8.2% (n=2,405) with sham purification: odds ratio 0.98 (95%CI: 0.92 to 1.05), P=0.609. Across all patients, the secondary composite outcome occurred in 5.5% (n=2,959 / 53,730) of active purification cases versus 5.6% (n=2,981 / 53,604) sham cases: odds ratio 0.98 (95% CI: 0.93 to 1.05), P=0.669). Treatment effect did not vary over the weeks in the randomized periods.
